title: Cash, Stash, or Slash: Joe Thuney
summary: As we continue to look at some key veterans on the Chicago Bears roster and whether the Bears should sign them to an extension (Cash), cut ties with them sooner rather than later (Slash), or play out another year and see where the player is at (Stash), we shift back to the offensive line and […]
full_text: SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 05: Joe Thuney during the 15th Annual NFL Honors at the Palace Of Fine Arts on February 05, 2026 in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we continue to look at some key veterans on the Chicago Bears roster and whether the Bears should sign them to an extension (Cash), cut ties with them sooner rather than later (Slash), or play out another year and see where the player is at (Stash), we shift back to the offensive line and look at Joe Thuney. After the trade with the Carolina Panthers that netted Caleb Williams, at this point I think you would have to say that Joe Thuney is Ryan Poles’ best acquisition. Thuney was acquired from the Kansas City Chiefs for just a fourth-round pick, and he helped rejuvenate a line that had been towards the bottom of the league for years and transform it into a top 5 line. Not only that, he was the recipient of the first-ever Protector award, given to the league’s best offensive lineman. In short, he was awesome. Joe Thuney: Cash This article is probably going to be shorter than a lot of others in this series just because there isn’t much debate here. Thuney is under contract through the 2027 season. That makes Thuney a prime extension candidate after this season. The Bears should sit Thuney down after this season and ask him how much longer he wants to play. There is no decision on the Bears’ side if they should keep Thuney or move on. They should keep him. The question is that Thuney will be 35 when this current contract expires, and you have to wonder how much longer he wants to play. Thuney hasn’t said much about his future in football; it may be that he will play out his current contract and retire after 2027, or it may be that he wants to sign another deal and stay in Chicago for a few more years. Nobody really knows what Thuney wants to do except for Joe Thuney. If Thuney wants to return, inking him to a 2-year extension after the 2026 season seems like a no-brainer for the Bears. Thuney has been remarkably durable, but if in his mid-to-late 30s his body starts breaking down and the contract doesn’t age well, you don’t worry about that one bit. It’s still worth the contract to try to keep him around, and like it was stated previously, there are no signs that Thuney is slowing down or becoming less durable. There are plenty of offensive linemen that excel late into their careers. Trent Williams is still elite at 38. Lane Johnson is still elite at 36 (although you have to wonder if the body is starting to break down). There are plenty of examples. Heck, the Bears stabilized their line a few years ago when they brought in 40-year-old Jason Peters to play LT. If Thuney wants to play, you pay him. At 34 or 35, Thuney isn’t going to be looking to make a massive contract. He will want fair market pay, and I expect negotiations would go pretty smoothly. Joe Thuney should be a Bear as long as Joe Thuney wants to play football. There really isn’t any other argument that holds a grain of salt.

title: Bears’ offense is back, Kaden Davis shines, Dayo Odeyingbo is motivated!
summary: After two physical practices in full gear, the Chicago Bears were just in shorts and shells today. It was a shorter practice, including some walk-through in the red zone, but the crispness from the offense definitely picked up after a rough outing on Tuesday. “Caleb Williams in 7 on 7 drill today so far: 8/9 […]
full_text: After two physical practices in full gear, the Chicago Bears were just in shorts and shells today. It was a shorter practice, including some walk-through in the red zone, but the crispness from the offense definitely picked up after a rough outing on Tuesday. “Caleb Williams in 7 on 7 drill today so far: 8/9 with TDs to Kyle Monangai, Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, and Kaden Davis,” per the Bear Report . “Very sharp in 7 on 7 today overall. Tyson Bagent, Case Keenum, and Miller Moss all had TDs. Think there was a total of 3 incompletions.” Every beat reporter in attendance raved about Kaden Davis’ sliding one-handed touchdown catch. Davis has been mentioned a few times during the first seven practices of camp, so he’s likely to be that “guy” this preseason. Even more so if the Bears share the video of today’s catch. Defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo is aware of the “Motivated Dayo” trend circulating on social media, and he laughed and said he was fine with it, saying , “It’s entertainment at the end of the day. That’s what football is about.” He added that rehabbing from an injury reminds him how much he wants to be out there and that “Being able to play football is a blessing.” Wideout Luther Burden III, who took a big shot yesterday, was at practice, and it was business as usual for him. Also, don’t forget that we’re just talking ’bout practice . A few other nuggets from the day. Left guard Joe Thuney and defensive tackle Grady Jarrett received veteran rest days today. With Thuney out, it was second-year pro Luke Newman filling in with the starters. ( link ) Braxton Jones had the bulk of the work at left tackle with the first string. However, at the start of practice, Theo Benedet was with the ones at LT, and Jedrick Wills Jr. was getting reps with the twos at right tackle. ( link ) Nickelback watch: Jaylon Jones is still NB1 with Josh Blackwell with the twos. ( link ) Also, “Dillon Thieneman says he’s cross-training a bit more in nickel and with man coverage,” per the Bear Report . “He’s been working with Al Harris on that.” Both T.J. Edwards (activated off the NFI) and Marlen Sewell (newly signed safety) got in their 40 up downs before practice. A few Bear defenders joined in. Dayo Odeyingbo has been lining up at defensive tackle in some obvious pass rush situations during the early days of camp. A recurring theme from players during the Ben Johnson era is truly fascinating. With Ben and this very solid group of assistants, one quality so many guys have responded to most is honesty. title: Bears’ Offense Seeking Explosives Over Efficiency
summary: Bears Offensive Coordinator Press Taylor met with the media this morning before training camp practice and gave everyone a glimpse into the mind of Head Coach Ben Johnson, along with some other noteworthy mentions of some key players. “I don’t think Ben has ever mentioned the word efficiency. We talk about explosive. We are trying […]
full_text: Aug 5, 2026; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor speaks during training camp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Bears Offensive Coordinator Press Taylor met with the media this morning before training camp practice and gave everyone a glimpse into the mind of Head Coach Ben Johnson, along with some other noteworthy mentions of some key players. “I don’t think Ben has ever mentioned the word efficiency. We talk about explosive. We are trying to attack a defense,” Taylor said. “I think there’s a perception by a lot of people [that] we’re going to run the ball, we’re going to stay efficient, we’re going to control the clock. We are looking to attack a defense.” “We’re looking to attack fronts, to expose space, to create run lanes, to create explosives.” Taylor reiterated. “I mean, we don’t look at the run game as a way to stay on track. We look at the run game as a way to attack defenses and really be explosive and continue to just put our foot on the gas the entire game.” Our own Jeff Berckes recently wrote a spectacular piece on the topic of explosives, and after watching the Bears offense last season, it’s no surprise to hear that our head coach is relaying the message of importance to his entire staff. Last season, Chicago was one of the most explosive teams in the league despite being near the bottom in 2024. #NFL Offensive Explosive Play Rates 2025 Explosive Rush Leaders: BAL, CHI Explosive Pass Leaders: NE, BUF pic.twitter.com/2tw9zczHAA — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) January 13, 2026 #NFL Explosive Play Rates 2024 Despite all the injuries, #SF remained an elite team in explosive plays on both sides of the ball. The #49ers finished the season with the 4th-highest offensive explosive play rate and the 3rd-lowest allowed on defense. pic.twitter.com/VigIpOOvgL — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) January 8, 2025 As you can see from the charts above and in reading JB’s article, and as we all saw last season with Swift and Monangai, explosives are far more than flea-flickers and Hail-Mary’s. The run game can create chunk plays, which keep defenses honest and exploit mismatches. Which leads me to the two players Press highlighted. Cole Kmet and Darnell Wright. This is the second coach to praise Kmet’s team-first mentality and laud his behavior and leadership. Easy to see why for those that have followed Kmet his entire career, but important, no less. Especially with two very young tight ends in his position room. TE Cole Kmet epitomizes what this #Bears Offense and Team is all about. The value of his versatility is matched only by his selflessness. Watch the two clips below…. • Cole Kmet on wanting to win more than he wants the ball. • OC Press Taylor on just how important Cole is… pic.twitter.com/YimFfCWzw9 — Herb Howard (@HerbHoward411) August 5, 2026 Surely, selflessness and ability contribute to more explosive plays. Which brings me to our newly extended STUD of a right tackle, Darnell Wright. Coach Taylor referred to Wright as one of the team’s best players and admitted to wanting to feature him and get behind he and right guard Jonah Jackson, but admitted even when plays aren’t designed to go behind those two behemoths, that “the ball tends to find its way back there because of the things he does well.” For the first time in a long time, Bears fans not only have a roster capable of taking the top off the defense and putting points on the board, but also has a mindset among their coaches to be explosive. Every. Single. Play. Bear down, everyone.

Edwards has been activated from the Active/Non-Football Injury List. Edwards was placed on the list before training camp with a minor muscle strain suffered while working out on his own after the OTAs and minicamps concluded. He had already returned to offseason activities after rehabbing his fractured fibula from the Wildcard game, so the strain was unrelated to that injury. The Bears will likely ramp T.J. up over the next day or two at training camp before clearing him for 100% participation. The Bears are in shorts and shells today and are scheduled for full pads tomorrow. Offensive tackle Ozzy Trapilo, nickleback Kyler Gordon, defensive lineman Shemar Turner, and linebackers Keyshaun Elliott and Noah Sewell remain on the Active/Physically Unable to Perform list. They can be at Halas Hall for meetings and rehab, but can’t get on the practice field until removed from the list.

title: Ryan Poles and the NFL Draft: Is he good enough? Part 2
summary: This article series began as an exploration of the drafting proficiency of the last three Chicago GMs. To learn more about the process and methodology, please refer back to Part 1. However, to quickly summarize the last piece–when indexed against players at the same position drafted in the same rounds, Ryan Poles is more “like” […]
full_text: This article series began as an exploration of the drafting proficiency of the last three Chicago GMs. To learn more about the process and methodology, please refer back to Part 1 . However, to quickly summarize the last piece–when indexed against players at the same position drafted in the same rounds, Ryan Poles is more “like” Jason Licht and Howie Roseman than he is like Ryan Pace or especially Phil Emery. He is drafting well, all things considered, and his performance has gone up each year. One very simple way of visualizing a GM’s performance is to group draft picks into thirds, categorizing each pick as in the upper, middle, or lower tier of performance by their draft slot. Poles has more upper-tier picks per draft than anyone but Howie Roseman, and he has more middle tier than anyone (though admittedly some of those are in the 40-50 range). He and Roseman’s first three years of independent control are alike in terms of how few truly bad picks they have, as well. They are also alike in terms of number of picks, which is remarkable given that this data includes the very “pick limited” class of 2024. However, that red bar is the strength and the weakness of what Ryan Poles has done to date. He has managed to claim value out of a majority of his picks, but fully half of the picks represented there are in fact below average , they are just not necessarily absolute misses. Still, compared to other GMs in comparable situations, he has two major accomplishments. The first is that he did not have a fall-off in his third year, which is promising. The second is that his overall performance has been strong in each of the available years. Not Uncommon Compared to the other GMs in this group and also compared to a random sampling of five other 3-year team stretches, Poles does not uniquely draft a position repeatedly. In other words, even though he drafted multiple offensive linemen in back-to-back years, so did other GMs. The same is true with wide receivers and corners (and so on). Likewise, the total positional spread and the offensive/defensive distribution of resources were fairly unremarkable. In many ways, Poles is “boring” when it comes to the draft, even if he seems to be better than average when considered “on net” instead of looking at specific struggles. When looked at without “games played” in the performance equation (in other words, when only production metrics and earned starts are used), his best results come from players who fell in the draft (with the single exception of Caleb Williams). However, that is also not unique to Ryan Poles. What is unusual is that all three of his “worst” results come from the third round. That leads to the most troubling part of this analysis. The Void Here are each of the first 24 selections made by Ryan Poles in order of draft priority, ranked against percentile performance for that position and draft round. That valley in the middle is noteworthy, and it’s concerning because many times the players taken in the third and fourth round end up being the backbone of NFL rosters. From #60-#140, Poles has drafted in the 31st percentile (by composite), and simply removing these picks from his draft performance would have him drafting in the 74th percentile overall. This data does not include Shemar Turner or Ruben Hyppolite II, who also fit within this range and who in their first year combined for 12 games, 1 start, and a total of two disruptive plays (both tackles for a loss by Turner). While it is difficult to assess from the outside why this void exists, it is worth looking at who Poles selects in this range. Two of these five players were reaches compared to consensus, two of them were players who had fallen compared to consensus, and one was picked broadly in range with consensus. Anecdotally, outside of this range, Austin Booker had fallen and Gervon Dexter was a reach, but both of those players turned out above-average for their draft position. Notably, however, in the case of four of the five of these players, multiple draft profiles mentioned a need for development. This suggests one possible explanation is that while the players themselves had potential, the Bears failed to develop them once they were on the team. If so, then at least for the future this issue might be resolved with the new coaching staff. By contrast, these could represent the “risky” picks that Poles takes once he has taken safer picks earlier on; in this case, it would seem that he is not judging those risks well. It is also possibly just an artifact of small sample size. Offense vs Defense During his time with head coach Matt Eberflus, Poles was able to draft well on offense in net, with a composite performance in the 68th percentile. However, that is not really an honest assessment of his ability. A slim majority (7 of 12) of his offensive selections were below the 50th percentile. However, his other selections have been quite good. His offensive drafting is, to borrow a term, K-shaped. His three biggest successes on the offensive side have been a pair of offensive linemen and a generational prospect at quarterback. Tellingly, he averaged two offensive linemen drafted per year, and only half were above average (and their unweighted percentile ranking is 51). In other words, there is little sign of “skill” in his offensive selections. Seven of his nine worst picks, by percentile, were on offense. Meanwhile, ten of his twelve defensive selections were above-average, with the only two outliers being Zacch Pickens and 7th-rounder Kendall Williamson. One obvious inference is that Poles relied heavily on the input of his (defensive-minded) head coach’s expertise. However, this could also be another line of evidence to support the idea that issues with drafting across these first three years were more about player development than player potential. Yes, the best offensive players managed to stand out. However, the weaker offensive players might not have been coached to their fullest potential, while the defensive players were better developed. The issue with this is that his work in the 5th round (with an average performance at the 70th percentile) undermines the idea that the problem in Round 3 and Round 4 is talent development. Conclusions Ryan Poles can be a frustrating GM for a fanbase, because while there are some things he demonstrably does well, there are other places where he instead struggles. It is tempting to call it all a matter of luck and say that he is “no better or worse” than most GMs. However, there are actual trends. The first is that he tends to be conservative in his approach, and as a result while his failures are blunted, so are his successes. He has a few true success stories, but many of those successes are a result of him setting up the conditions for his success outside of the actual evaluation of players–the trade with the Panthers, the exchange of older or more expensive players for extra draft picks, and taking multiple swings at positions. Yet even when those elements are removed, he is drafting better than the league average by multiple measures. That suggests that if he can continue to do so even as his draft capital decreases, he should be able to continue to improve the team. What Poles does not seem to be able to do, yet, is stack multiple high-leverage successes in a single draft. Added to the other components of team-building where there is also room for improvement (such as free agency), this means there is reasonable fear over whether or not the team can continue to improve now that it has notched its first playoff victory over the last three general managers. The final part of this series will be an extended necropsy on the Ryan Pace era in Chicago with implications for the Bears moving forward.

title: Bengals safety Bryan Cook is embracing his leadership role
summary: At practice on Tuesday, cornerback DJ Turner was beaten deep by Ja’Marr Chase on what ended up being an incomplete pass. Turner didn’t have time to get down on himself because free-agent safety acquisition Bryan Cook was quickly by his side to give him a word of encouragement. Then, on the very next play, Boye […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals safety Bryan Cook (6) cheers after breaking up a play during practice at the Paycor Stadium practice facility in downtown Cincinnati on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co At practice on Tuesday, cornerback DJ Turner was beaten deep by Ja’Marr Chase on what ended up being an incomplete pass. Turner didn’t have time to get down on himself because free-agent safety acquisition Bryan Cook was quickly by his side to give him a word of encouragement. Then, on the very next play, Boye Mafe, another free agent acquisition, beat Orlando Brown Jr. around the edge and forced Joe Burrow to throw an errant pass earlier than he wanted. Cook stepped in front of the pass, picked it off, and took it back for what would have been a touchdown had it been a real game. Later in the locker room, Cook reflected on the moment, showcasing his leadership, not only verbally, but with action. “For the most part, it’s just being aggressive, attention to detail, flying around, playing as one, and also being my brother’s keeper,” he said in the locker room after practice . “I know we’re all tired, but make a play. Any given moment, it could happen. I can be tired and have a great break at the post, and then Dexter Lawrence can get a sack. Things like that, it boosts the whole morale of a defense.” The Bengals’ defense has largely been to blame for the team missing the playoffs over the last two seasons. Sure, if they bounced their way one or two times in either season, they could have backed their way into the playoffs, but a team can win if they allow opposing teams to score 30 or more points as often as they did. This offseason, though, the Bengals’ front office took the big swing generations of fans have been asking for. They not only traded the No. 10 pick to the Giants for Lawrence, but they signed Cook, Mafe, Jonathan Allen and Kyle Dugger. Combined with this year’s draft class, the entire defense, except for linebacker, has been reshaped. With Cook’s leadership in the secondary and with the monster that is Lawrence soaking up blockers meant to get to linebackers, the defense will hopefully transform from a liability to a strength.
author: Jason Garrison

summary: The Cincinnati Bengals went all-in on fixing their defense this offseason. Despite losing Trey Hendrickson to the Baltimore Ravens, the Bengals made several additions all across the defense to try to fix the unit that shouldered the blame for missing the postseason the last two seasons. Included in those acquisitions was pass rusher Boye Mafe, […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 16: Myles Murphy #99 of the Cincinnati Bengals pressures Mason Rudolph #2 of the Pittsburgh Steelers during the third quarter at Acrisure Stadium on November 16, 2025 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals went all-in on fixing their defense this offseason. Despite losing Trey Hendrickson to the Baltimore Ravens, the Bengals made several additions all across the defense to try to fix the unit that shouldered the blame for missing the postseason the last two seasons. Included in those acquisitions was pass rusher Boye Mafe, who was basically signed as a replacement for Hendrickson. They will also return 2025 first-round pick Shemar Stewart when he returns from his hyperextended knee suffered early in training camp. 2023 first-rounder Myles Murphy is also back and likely motivated after his fifth-year option wasn’t picked up. Also joining the rotation is rookie and former SEC Defensive Player of the Year, Cashius Howell. CBS Sports’ Carter Bahns isn’t very confident in the Cincinnati pass rush this season. He recently released his rankings of all 32 pass rush groups in the NFL and slotted the Bengals near the bottom of the league at 29th. “While the rest of the Bengals’ defense improved on paper this offseason, the edge rusher group said farewell to its leader, Trey Hendrickson. Mafe is an upside-oriented addition who will not fully replace Hendrickson’s pass-rushing prowess, but who displayed flashes of greatness as a young starter for the Seattle Seahawks. The rest of the crew, plus second-round pick Cashius Howell, is extremely young. Cincinnati is banking on its last few drafts starting to pay off. It just might pay dividends, but it is impossible to know for sure until it actually happens,“ Bahn wrote. To be fair, there are quite a few unknowns along the defensive front and specifically at pass rusher, but 29 still feels awfully low when you consider the drastic improvements to the interior defensive line. Dexter Lawrence II should draw a lot of double teams and free up pass rushers to get home. Preseason rankings are just that, preseason predictions. In just over a month, the Bengals’ defense will have a chance to change that narrative on the field.

title: Dexter Lawrence is already making life miserable for the Bengals’ offense, and they couldn’t be happier
summary: When the Cincinnati Bengals traded a first-round pick to acquire Dexter Lawrence this offseason, the expectation was that the three-time Pro Bowler would transform a defense that desperately needed a game-wrecker in the middle. One week into training camp, it sounds like that transformation is already underway. From Joe Burrow to Ja’Marr Chase to the offensive line […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - JULY 29: Dexter Lawrence II #97 of the Cincinnati Bengals signs autographs during the Cincinnati Bengals Training Camp at Kettering Health Practice Fields on July 29, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Cincinnati Bengals traded a first-round pick to acquire Dexter Lawrence this offseason, the expectation was that the three-time Pro Bowler would transform a defense that desperately needed a game-wrecker in the middle. One week into training camp, it sounds like that transformation is already underway. From Joe Burrow to Ja’Marr Chase to the offensive line tasked with blocking him every day, the reviews have been remarkably consistent: Lawrence has been every bit as disruptive as advertised. And while it has made practices far more difficult for Cincinnati’s offense, it’s exactly the kind of challenge the Bengals believe will make them a better football team when the games begin. The loudest endorsement came from Chase, who didn’t mince words when describing the veteran defensive tackle’s impact. “Honestly, he’s been terrorizing practice,” Chase said, via Yahoo! Sports. “I can honestly say that.” That’s about as glowing a compliment as a wide receiver can give a defensive tackle. Joe Burrow has already felt Lawrence’s presence Burrow echoed that sentiment after practice when asked about the newest centerpiece of Cincinnati’s defensive front. The franchise quarterback admitted Lawrence has forced the offense to speed up its operation because the pocket simply doesn’t stay clean for very long. "Dex is just so big, he makes throwing over the middle a little more difficult." Joe Burrow has had to adjust to the addition of Dexter Lawrence on the Bengals' D-line 😂 🎤: @EvanWashburn pic.twitter.com/mOzDifZHq4 — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) August 3, 2026 As Burrow explained in the NFL on CBS interview clip via Evan Washburn, the offense has to “get that thing out” faster when Lawrence collapses the middle of the pocket, adding that the All-Pro defensive tackle has looked the part during the opening days of camp. It’s the type of praise that carries extra weight coming from one of the NFL’s premier quarterbacks. Burrow has faced elite interior defenders throughout his career, and Lawrence has quickly reminded everyone why he has long been considered among the league’s most dominant defensive tackles. The offensive line is embracing the challenge Perhaps no Bengal has had a tougher assignment than center Ted Karras, who has lined up across from Lawrence throughout camp. Rather than complain about the impossible task, Karras has welcomed it. Earlier this week, Karras called Lawrence “probably the best nose tackle in the last 30 years,” explaining that practicing against a player of that caliber every day will only sharpen Cincinnati’s offensive line heading into the season. He also compared the challenge to practicing against some of the dominant New England Patriots defenses from earlier in his career, saying Lawrence has immediately elevated the competitiveness of practice. Cincinnati offensive guard Dalton Risner echoed Karras’ sentiments about Lawrence’s presence through camp. “There’s certain guys in this league like Dexter who wreck a whole game play, and you have to do everything around them, and you change everything you’re doing,” Risner said, via Yahoo! Sports. “You’re going to have to change how you block against certain guys. “He’s just making us do it really early and really often.” That’s exactly what the Bengals envisioned when they made the blockbuster trade. A defense that suddenly looks different The Bengals spent much of the offseason overhauling a defense that struggled throughout 2025. Lawrence’s arrival has quickly become the centerpiece of that rebuild. Reports from camp have consistently highlighted a defense winning its share of team periods, with Lawrence creating havoc in both the running and passing game while helping open opportunities for the linebackers and edge rushers around him. That impact extends beyond the stat sheet. When elite offensive players like Burrow and Chase are openly talking about how disruptive one defender has been, it says plenty about what Lawrence has brought to Cincinnati. Offensive Coordinator Dan Pitcher added that Lawrence is a “nightmare” for units going up against “Sexy Dexy”. Training camp is designed to make teams uncomfortable. Through the first week, nobody has embodied that philosophy more than Dexter Lawrence. If his practice performances are any indication, opposing offenses may soon find themselves echoing the same sentiment Ja’Marr Chase delivered so succinctly: He’s been terrorizing people. “Better bring your f-ing shit when you’re going against Dexter Lawrence.” Ted Karras being tested daily against the stud DT. Karras compared it to going up against the 2016 Patriots in practice. pic.twitter.com/j2GMQscxmB — Mike Petraglia (@Trags) August 1, 2026

title: Zac Taylor discusses expectations for the 2026 Cincinnati Bengals
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have all the ingredients for a bounce-back season. At least on paper. But if you ask head coach Zac Taylor, that’s exactly where the conversation should stop for now. Speaking with ESPN Bengals beat writer Ben Baby ahead of the 2026 season, Taylor said there’s genuine excitement surrounding the organization, but he made it […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals have all the ingredients for a bounce-back season. At least on paper. But if you ask head coach Zac Taylor, that’s exactly where the conversation should stop for now. Speaking with ESPN Bengals beat writer Ben Baby ahead of the 2026 season, Taylor said there’s genuine excitement surrounding the organization, but he made it clear that optimism alone won’t win games. “We’re putting in all the work we possibly can to make sure we have a great year and get back to those years that we really cherished as coaches and players,” Taylor said. “But there is a lot of work we have got to put in over the course of August to get there.” "You can feel the genuine excitement for the season. … Personnel, ownership, they've given us everything we need to succeed, and now we just got to go do it." —Head coach Zac Taylor on the Bengals' expectations ahead of the season ✍️ pic.twitter.com/7pyY8eH67w — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) August 1, 2026 It’s a measured message from a coach whose team enters the season carrying significant expectations after an aggressive offseason. Taylor praised everyone in the organization—from ownership to the personnel department—for giving the coaching staff the resources needed to compete, but stressed that turning talent into victories is now the coaches’ and players’ responsibility. “Got a lot of players, got to utilize them the right way,” Taylor stressed. It’s a philosophy Bengals fans have already seen in training camp. Coaches have been experimenting with personnel packages while evaluating how best to maximize both established stars and emerging contributors before Week 1. Taylor cautioned against putting too much stock in offseason practices. “On paper, things look great,” he said. “The attitude is great, the energy is great. Until we really put in that work and see where our team’s at, it’s impossible to say where we stand.” That humility comes after a disappointing 2025 campaign in which Cincinnati finished 6-11 and missed the playoffs. Taylor has repeatedly used last season as motivation, even reminding players of that record at the start of training camp as the team looks to recapture the standard it set during its AFC championship runs. As Taylor put it, Cincinnati has about five weeks of work remaining before the games begin to count. By then, the discussion will turn to whether the promise the Bengals showed in the preseason can translate into victories.

title: Bengals News: Training camp continues
summary: The Bengals continue to plow their way through training camp, now in Week 2, as they prepare for their first preseason game next Thursday. full_text: Cincinnati Bengals defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II (97) unwraps his fingers during practice on Tuesday, June 9, 2026, at Kettering Health Practice Fields in downtown Cincinnati. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Bengals continue to plow their way through training camp, now in Week 2, as they prepare for their first preseason game next Thursday. The pads were on Tuesday, and they’ll be on Thursday and Friday as well. Then they’ll have one more camp practice before their preseason game against the Lions. All eyes are on the defense, and by extension, Dexter Lawrence. He’s the new face of the defense, and has looked dominant in camp, according to some eyewitness accounts. His presence on the defensive line has, in theory, given linebackers Demetrius Knight Jr. and Barrett Carter the ability to play more free. The additions of Bryan Cook in the secondary and Boye Mafe and Jonathan Allen on the line will hopefully pay dividends as well. The offense has been nothing to overlook either. Joe Burrow has shown his connection with Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins, the best wide receiver duo in the league, is just as strong as ever. Chase Brown, who’s on a contract year, is poised to earn the big bucks if he can continue to improve not only as a runner, but as a receiver. On top of all that, the offense has been running quite a bit of 13 personnel with three tight ends on the field, and Burrow under center. So yeah, there have only been a handful of practices, but a lot has happened. Reds pay visit to Bengals at training camp in ‘super cool experience’ “I admire [Chase’s] work and like him a lot as a player,” Sal Stewart said. “I love when he said, ‘I’m like 7/11, I’m always open.’ And it’s true! He is always open. He’s obviously the best wide receiver in the league so it was cool and I love watching him play.” While all eyes are on Sexy Dexy, and for good reason, the addition of Cook can not be overlooked. He was the best safety on the market this offseason. He’s a sure tackler, a two-time Super Bowl champion and he knows how to communicate in the secondary, a skill he developed and refined as one of the leaders in Kansas City’s secondary . Oh, and he’s a former Cincinnati Bearcat. DEXTER LAWRENCE ‘TERRORIZING PRACTICE’ AT BENGALS TRAINING CAMP “When you have a man as big as (Lawrence), the quick twitch and the speed they’re able to play with just disarms you,” Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher told Jori Epstein of Yahoo! Sports. “I don’t know what you do to counteract that other than you just really focus on the technique of this interior line and you got to be really cognizant of what types of schemes you’re trying to run and how often that guy’s truly one-on-one. Running sideways and backward at quarterback in the NFL is a good way to not play very long. So it’s a problem.” More on Cook’s leadership as a huge reason why the Bengals’ defense has shown up through the first few sessions of training camp. After DJ Turner was beat by Chase on a deep ball that fell incomplete, it was Cook who was hyping him up. Just a couple plays later, Cook stepped in front of a pass thrown early because Mafe got in his face, and took it back for a pick six . Hopefully Cook is finally the Bengals’ answer to “how do we move on from Jessie Bates?” As the preseason approaches, since there is no practice today (Wednesday), answer this simple question: How much should Burrow play during the team’s three preseason games? Sound off!

title: Browns QB Dillon Gabriel quietly putting in the work at camp
summary: Cleveland Browns quarterback Dillon Gabriel has been the invisible man in the early days of training camp as the third man in a depressing two-man quarterback competition. Some of that is to be expected given that veteran Deshaun Watson is healthy enough to participate after missing all of last year with a twice-torn Achilles tendon. […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - AUGUST 03: Dillon Gabriel #6 of the Cleveland Browns throws a pass during the Cleveland Browns Training Camp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on August 03, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Cleveland Browns quarterback Dillon Gabriel has been the invisible man in the early days of training camp as the third man in a depressing two-man quarterback competition. Some of that is to be expected given that veteran Deshaun Watson is healthy enough to participate after missing all of last year with a twice-torn Achilles tendon. And Gabriel did not exactly light up the NFL in his six starts as a rookie, completing just 59.5 percent of his passes and seeing the Browns win just one of his starts. Gabriel was statistically better than fellow rookie Shedeur Sanders in just about every metric that matters, however, so one could begrudge him for feeling a bit left out with the spotlight shining so brightly on Watson and Sanders. But Gabriel does not seem wired that way, at least outwardly, as on Wednesday he said he never felt “disrespected” and that he understands the NFL is a business. He also spoke confidently about being able to pick up what head coach Todd Monken wants from the offense given the similarities to what Gabriel ran in college (quote via a team-provided transcript): “I don’t think picking up an offense has ever been a problem for me. I think conceptually, if you see it, a lot of people are on the same (stuff); it’s just how you call it and how you get to things. In man versus zone, or a two-high one-high, do you want an all-call where you can play it split field on one play, or do you want to get to a premier play where there are multiple winners against a certain coverage? “I think I take that kind of attitude toward it, plus my time with Coach (Dan) Lanning — whatever that Georgia tree is — and Coach Monken being there, I think there’s some similarities. Even in practice and how we’ve seen our offense, it’s kind of similar to Oregon.” Being comfortable in the offense could conceivably give Gabriel a leg up on the competition, and the fact that he is going about his business has not gone unnoticed by Monken, as he explained on Wednesday : “One thing Dillon does a really good job of is he’s very even-keeled. First of all, he’s got a great personality; he’s fun to be around. You wouldn’t know it unless you’ve been around him. He seems stoic, but no, he’s actually very funny, has a great personality, and he’s handled this situation with unbelievable class. “Every player wants to compete, and he hasn’t really had the opportunity in terms of the number of reps. He’s had a chance to compete just with a different number of reps. So, I think he’s done an unbelievable job that way, and for the lack of reps, he does a great job carrying over the meetings to the field. He does a great job with a limited amount of reps, which is a credit to him.” The competition to be the Week 1 starter for the Browns will still likely come down to Watson or Sanders unless something drastic happens between now and the opener against the Jacksonville Jaguars. But given that this is the Browns, they will likely need multiple quarterbacks once again this fall, and Gabriel staying ready could pay off for him at some point before the end of the regular season.

title: Browns QBs: What could lead Dillon Gabriel back to challenge Sanders, Watson
summary: The biggest storyline entering this season’s training camp was whether Shedeur Sanders or Deshaun Watson would earn the starting quarterback job for Week 1. Unexpectedly, Dillon Gabriel’s name has already started to generate some buzz early in camp and has shifted the conversation slightly. Head coach Todd Monken mentioned to the media that if Gabriel continues to stack good […]
full_text: The biggest storyline entering this season’s training camp was whether Shedeur Sanders or Deshaun Watson would earn the starting quarterback job for Week 1. Unexpectedly, Dillon Gabriel’s name has already started to generate some buzz early in camp and has shifted the conversation slightly. Head coach Todd Monken mentioned to the media that if Gabriel continues to stack good days, he will get more reps. Early reports are showing impressive development from Gabriel. On the other hand, both Watson and Sanders have received significant criticism for their performances in camp thus far. It’s still too early to draw any conclusions, and plenty can change, but Gabriel’s emergence as a contender is an unexpected development. At the end of the day, the coaching staff needs to start whoever gives the team the best chance to win. If that ends up being Gabriel based on the product he is putting out on the field day after day in training camp, then the team should start him. Ultimately, if he wins that job, it will mean that he truly proved he deserves to be there. Let me know what you think in the comments – Should Gabriel start over Watson & Sanders?

summary: The Cleveland Browns saw a need for additional depth at defensive tackle and claimed Coziah Izzard off waivers from the Arizona Cardinals. full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 10: Aaron Anderson #85 of the Cleveland Browns catches a pass during the Cleveland Browns Mandatory Minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 10, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Cleveland Browns saw a need for additional depth at defensive tackle and claimed Coziah Izzard off waivers from the Arizona Cardinals. The Cardinals have a logjam at DT and released Izzard on Monday. This is the third free agent defender added in the last few days for the Browns roster, including a recent UFL star . In a corresponding move, Cleveland waived WR Aaron Anderson with an injury designation. Anderson, a UDFA this offseason, had made a number of exciting plays already in training camp but was injured in practice on Tuesday, and quickly waived Tuesday afternoon. RELATED: FANS FEEL GOOD ABOUT DEFENSIVE LINE WITH ADDITION OF VERSE Arizona cut Izzard (6’-3”, 305 pounds) to make room for a kickoff return man. Izzard had been inserted into the Cardinals’ depth chart, which currently has eight DTs on the training camp roster. Izzard went undrafted in last year’s NFL draft before signing with the Kansas City Chiefs after a stellar college campaign at Penn State, where he was referred to as “an athletic freak.” Despite having a decent camp with KC, he was released on the final cutdown day, then signed to the practice squad, and later waived. Four days later, the New Orleans Saints signed him to their practice squad, where he spent all of 2025. Although he inked a reserve/futures contract in January, the Saints released him on June 17. The Cardinals were seeking to fill the depth void when one of their draft picks became injured, a defensive tackle, and signed Izzard after a tryout with other players last week. Coziah Izzard. Just destroyed a play by himself — Max Ralph (@maxralph_) November 26, 2022 In high school, Izzard was named All-Conference for all four years. His school won the state championship in his senior year. He had 23 major-program college football offers. Because of the pandemic, Izzard was a fifth-year senior. He played in 50 games with just seven starts, 78 total tackles, 17.5 tackles for loss, 9 sacks, 0 batted passes, and 2 forced fumbles. Currently at defensive tackle for the Browns are: RDT: Mason Graham, backup: Adin Huntington, depth: Sam Kamara, Travis Bell LDT: Maliek Collins, backup: Mike Hall, depth: Kalia Davis, Elijah Chatman, Coziah Izzard Typically, most NFL clubs keep four DTs and five defensive ends. The defensive tackles are then rotated in during each game in order to keep them fresh.

title: Cowboys news: Jaydon Blue understood the lesson
summary: One thing is for certain for the Dallas Cowboys, second-year running back Jaydon Blue is on a mission to be a contributor after a rough rookie campaign. Linebackers DeMarvion Overshown and rookie Jaishawn Barham are having good training camps, and the versatility of both will be used a lot in 2026. Christian Parker is gearing […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Dallas, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys running back Jaydon Blue (23) goes through a drill during practice at the Ford Center at the Star Training Facility in Frisco, Texas. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images One thing is for certain for the Dallas Cowboys, second-year running back Jaydon Blue is on a mission to be a contributor after a rough rookie campaign. Linebackers DeMarvion Overshown and rookie Jaishawn Barham are having good training camps, and the versatility of both will be used a lot in 2026. Christian Parker is gearing up for his first year of calling plays as a defensive coordinator, and according to him, his unit is taking the right steps. Ryan Flournoy is the WR3 in Dallas, but he’s poised to elevate his play this year. Here’s your Cowboys’ news for Thursday. Cowboys’ Jaydon Blue understands his Year 2 assignment: ‘I took the lessons to heart’ – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com Jaydon Blue had high expectations as a rookie, but things didn’t go as planned for multiple reasons. Now, he’s ready to be a difference maker in 2026. “I’m just [focused on] stacking these good days out here,” said Blue, following the second Cowboys’ padded practice in which he shined again. “I’ve just been more intentional. Like I said, this offseason, my main priority was making sure that I stayed in the playbook and was doing things that the coach was asking me to do.” Cowboys MLB DeMarvion Overshown has rave reviews for new DC Christian Parker at training camp – SportsDay Staff, Dallas Morning News Christian Parker has a lot of support in his defensive coordinator position, but it is his first year calling plays. However, linebacker DeMarvion Overshown says believe the hype. DeMarvion Overshown: “He’s a competitor, just like us. He feels like he’s putting on a helmet and shoulder pads as well when we come out here to get ready for practice. In meeting rooms, he’s challenging us to know what the rest of the defense is doing, like he wants everyone to be able to think like they’re a coach out there. What stood out after Cowboys’ padded practices? 2 players who could elevate the offense – Jon Machota, The Athletic The Cowboys have one of the top offenses in the NFL. It may be even better this season if a few players take a leap. Ryan Flournoy Everyone knows the importance of CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens to Dallas’ passing game. But Flournoy has shown that he’s ready to build on what he did after his breakout performance in Week 5 last year against the New York Jets. In 16 games last season, Flournoy had 40 catches for 475 yards and four touchdowns. He’s got a chance to be closer to the 700-800 yard range this season as Dallas’ clear No. 3 wide receiver. Christian Parker pleased with Cowboys defense’s progress early in training camp – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com The Cowboys had one of the worst defenses in team history in 2025. This prompted them to hire Christian Parker as their new defensive coordinator, and things are running smoothly so far in training camp. “I think we’re embracing the play style that we want to stay with,” Parker said. “I think guys are really just trying to harp on the details and get the next level of knowledge to the defense that we’re really focusing on. We talked about getting your undergraduate degree in OTAs, and now we’re working towards our masters. That’s more of an accelerated program, so we’ve got to get going quick. The guys are doing a great job.” It looks like the Dallas Cowboys have a secret pass rushing weapon, and they’re showing it in training camp – Mauricio Rodriguez, AtoZ Sports Dallas didn’t blitz linebacker DeMarvion Overshown that much last season like they did in 2024 under Mike Zimmer. Christian Parker wants to take advantage of that part of his game again. There’s still plenty to figure out with Overshown. The biggest question remains whether he can play middle linebacker with the physicality the position requires. Can he take on climbing offensive linemen at the second level, something far more common at MIKE than at weakside linebacker where he had more open space to operate? There was a play earlier this week where left tackle Tyler Guyton climbed to the second level and swallowed Overshown whole. That part of his game remains to be answered. But one thing is clear: Overshown as a blitzer is back. Cowboys rookie Jaishawn Barham’s versatility becoming a ‘cheat code’ for Christian Parker – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News Jaishawn Barham has done a nice job making himself known at training camp. He played both linebacker and edge at Michigan, and defensive coordinator Christian Parker is salivating over he’s versatility. “Him playing both is one of his cheat codes that he has,” Parker said. “He’s played equal amount of snaps almost at Maryland and Michigan [at inside linebacker], so he’s been exposed to it. So it’s not like he’s seeing things that he hasn’t seen before from that perspective. … I think that he is a fast processor.” Daily discussion question: How much will you watch of the HOF game?

title: Christian Parker takeaways so far at Oxnard
summary: When the Cowboys hired Christian Parker as defensive coordinator, they weren’t just seeking a new coach. They wanted someone capable of rebuilding a defense that finished 2025 as one of the NFL’s worst units, while also developing a young secondary packed with potential. Just over a week into training camp in Oxnard means it’s still […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Oxnard, CA, USA; Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker at training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect When the Cowboys hired Christian Parker as defensive coordinator, they weren’t just seeking a new coach. They wanted someone capable of rebuilding a defense that finished 2025 as one of the NFL’s worst units, while also developing a young secondary packed with potential. Just over a week into training camp in Oxnard means it’s still early, but many of the first signs have been extremely encouraging. Christian Parker coaching up Cobie Durant and Daron Bland #Dallascowboys pic.twitter.com/vltsKrsspK — Nicole Hutchison (@nhutchisontv) August 1, 2026 The biggest takeaway has been how quickly players have embraced Parker’s coaching style. Rather than creating a passive practice environment, Parker has encouraged constant competition between the offense and defense. Players have described practices as iron sharpening iron, with the defense feeding off the challenge of facing Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens every day. That competitive atmosphere has noticeably increased the energy level of camp and has created an environment where every rep matters. Sam Williams sniffing out the Jaydon Blue run #Dallascowboys pic.twitter.com/MrNud6i100 — Nicole Hutchison (@nhutchisontv) August 4, 2026 KaVontae Turpin vs. Shavon Revel pic.twitter.com/XQeDKZZcAu — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) August 4, 2026 One of the first things that stands out about Christian Parker’s defense is the importance he places on communication. Every player in the secondary is expected to know not only their own assignment but also how the coverage changes based on motion, formations and offensive adjustments. That has created a defense where players are constantly talking before the snap instead of waiting for the play to unfold. Parker’s experience developing defensive backs is showing through the way Dallas is using its personnel, with safeties and cornerbacks moving into different roles rather than being limited to a single position. Rookie Caleb Downs has been one of the biggest examples of that flexibility, spending time as a deep safety, working closer to the line of scrimmage and lining up in the slot depending on the situation. Malachi Lawrence with the pressure, Caleb Downs with the near INT. The two first round picks on the play. pic.twitter.com/S9UJDcgSQE — Joseph Hoyt (@JoeJHoyt) August 1, 2026 The secondary has arguably been the biggest success story of camp so far. After struggling through much of last season, the defensive backfield has looked far more confident and competitive in Oxnard. Shavon Revel is slowly showing why the Cowboys are so excited about his future by matching receivers physically throughout practice, while DaRon Bland looks fully recovered and back to playing with the instincts that made him one of the league’s most dangerous ballhawks. Cobie Durant has wasted little time making an impression after arriving in Dallas, and Julius Wood has consistently shown his willingness to play downhill and finish through contact. Those performances carried into the first padded practice, where the defensive backs repeatedly challenged throws, closed passing windows and highlighted the day with Durant’s interception in the red zone. Cobie Durant downfield PBU pic.twitter.com/Gj8rp3xDhN — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) August 4, 2026 pic.twitter.com/oXoBKFyU2O — Clarence Hill Jr (@clarencehilljr) August 5, 2026 Another encouraging development has been how comfortable the entire group already looks despite learning a new defensive system. Mistakes that often accompany a scheme change have been relatively limited, with the secondary playing faster because players appear confident in what they are being asked to do, and that’s thanks to the work Parker has done preparing the guys upfront. Rather than making tackles after completions, defenders have frequently been in position to contest passes before receivers can secure the football. The safety group has also demonstrated far more flexibility, regularly changing responsibilities based on offensive looks instead of remaining in static alignments. Parker’s personality has also left an impression on the practice field. He coaches with energy, demands attention to detail and isn’t afraid to hold players accountable when standards aren’t met or things fall out of line, we’re looking at you Donovan Ezeiruaku. At the same time, he’s quick to celebrate effort, turnovers and winning reps, creating a competitive atmosphere that has spread throughout the defense. His message has been simple from the start, improvement has to happen every day, because standing still means falling behind Donovan Ezeiruaku was pulled from practice by Brian Schottenheimer after getting into it with Terence Steele. He spoke with Will McClay for a moment before Todd Williams walked him off the field. pic.twitter.com/RhPIGKAhEY — Bobby Belt (@BobbyBeltTX) August 4, 2026 Even with all the positive signs, there is still plenty of work to do. Training camp practices can only reveal so much, and preseason games will provide the first real opportunity to see how the defense performs against unfamiliar opponents and how the down roster guys can find a place on the defense. The Cowboys’ offense has still produced explosive plays at times, particularly when Prescott has been well protected, reminding everyone that the installation process is far from complete. The next step for Parker’s unit will be proving that the communication, versatility and aggressive style on display in Oxnard translate once the games begin to count. Caleb Downs and Christian Parker getting in some work after practice pic.twitter.com/ra1Tt9l1En — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) August 1, 2026 Even so, the early signs are difficult to ignore. The secondary looks more connected, younger players are developing rapidly, veterans appear fully invested in Parker’s message, and the overall energy surrounding the defense feels dramatically different from a year ago. If those trends continue once the games begin, the Cowboys may finally have found the defensive leader capable of unlocking a defense that should hold its own and create one of the most talented secondaries they’ve assembled in years. Dak Prescott and Christian Parker sharing some laughs before practice pic.twitter.com/hF3xcVNy1d — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) July 30, 2026
author: Mike Poland

title: Malik Davis is falling behind in Cowboys’ RB competition
summary: Malik Davis is back for his fifth training camp with the Dallas Cowboys, coming off the best season of his career. But while the running back gave us a feel-good story in 2025, that momentum doesn’t seem to be carrying into Oxnard so far. As things stand, Davis may once again leave camp without a […]
full_text: Aug 1, 2026; Oxnard, CA, USA; Dallas Cowboys running back Malik Davis (20) carries the ball at training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Malik Davis is back for his fifth training camp with the Dallas Cowboys, coming off the best season of his career. But while the running back gave us a feel-good story in 2025, that momentum doesn’t seem to be carrying into Oxnard so far. As things stand, Davis may once again leave camp without a roster spot. Switching to Tony Pollard’s old #20 this offseason hasn’t brought Davis any closer to the backup job. Thus far, Jaydon Blue has been given clear RB2 treatment behind Javonte Williams. And while Davis may be the third-man up, we’re hearing good things about prospects Phil Mafah and Israel Abanikanda as reports come from Oxnard. RB drills usually go in depth chart order .. Today, it’s 33-23-20 pic.twitter.com/4FEVlmLfr3 — Nick Eatman (@nickeatman) August 4, 2026 Phil Mafah with the nice vision and cut. also: i wonder if, at full speed, who would’ve won that between him and Cobie Durant. 🤔 #Cowboys pic.twitter.com/7HwOSqZkdB — Patrik [No C] Walker (@VoiceOfTheStar) August 4, 2026 ** RB Israel Abanikanda is someone to watch. Unsure how he makes the 53-man roster, but he is a guy that could have an eye-catching preseason. He has quickness and can see the hole quickly. — Todd Archer (@toddarcher) August 3, 2026 I think this was Israel Abanikanda https://t.co/0HvQk2qMAN — Tom Downey (@WhatGoingDowney) August 4, 2026 Davis has been down this road before. In fact, four times before. While Davis always looks solid with the ball in his hands, it’s never been enough to outshine some of the other RBs in camp. In his early years, Davis kept losing out to Rico Dowdle because he couldn’t match Dowdle’s abilities as a blocker and special teamer. Unfortunately for him, Davis’ blocking woes have already been on display this summer. Probably a sack from Shemar James here vs Malik Davis. https://t.co/VDQB96ccSG — Mauricio Rodríguez (@MauNFL) August 3, 2026 Turning 28 this November, Davis is obviously not a developmental guy anymore. He has to be clearly better than these younger prospects, probably winning the RB2 job outright if he wants to make the roster. But with Blue off to a hot start in camp and guys like Abanikanda and Mafah also showing well, it’s hard to imagine Davis faring any better in this camp than he has in the ones before it. It’s going to sting for fans who rightfully developed a soft spot for Davis after last year’s heroics. Finding his way back on the roster after Miles Sanders’ injury and Blue’s delayed development, Davis had a big play in Dallas’ Thanksgiving victory over Kansas City, then led the rushing attack in the Christmas win over Washington. In front of huge national audiences, Davis shined and did a lot to raise his profile, at least with Cowboys fans. Still, for the last four years, the Cowboys have consistently decided not to put Malik Davis on the 53 unless injuries forced their hand. As long as the RB room doesn’t have a sudden run of bad medical luck, we seem to be trending in that direction again in 2026. It’s going to sting for some, but we can find comfort in the probability that Davis’ fall means younger guys with broader skills are moving up the ladder, and hopefully improving Dallas’ overall depth at running back.

title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 39
summary: It is Day 39 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA - NOVEMBER 8: Quarterback Tony Romo #9 of the Dallas Cowboys scrambles during the game against the Philadelphia Eagles on November 8, 2009 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Cowboys won 20-16. (Photo by Drew Hallowell/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is Day 39 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. Get ready Cowboys fans for Day 39 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit an exorcism game for an entire generation of Cowboys fans. Dallas entered the 2009 postseason carrying 13 years of January frustration, six consecutive playoff defeats and all the baggage attached to Tony Romo’s previous postseason failures. By the end of the night, none of that mattered. Saturday, January 9, 2010 — 8:00 p.m. ET Cowboys Stadium, Arlington, Texas Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 34, Philadelphia Eagles 14 The matchup itself felt unusual because the teams had played in the same stadium only six days earlier. Dallas had shut out Philadelphia 24-0 in the regular-season finale to win the NFC East, dropping the Eagles from a potential first-round bye to the sixth seed. That created an immediate rematch in the Wild Card round, with Philadelphia returning to Arlington and insisting the previous result would not be repeated. The first quarter ended scoreless, but Dallas had already established control through long possessions and defensive pressure. The Cowboys finally broke through early in the second quarter after a deep throw toward Miles Austin drew a 40-yard pass-interference penalty against Sheldon Brown. From the one-yard line, Romo found reserve tight end John Phillips for the opening touchdown and a 7-0 lead. Philadelphia answered almost immediately. Andy Reid brought Michael Vick into the game, and Vick launched a deep pass to rookie Jeremy Maclin. Cornerback Mike Jenkins lost his footing, allowing Maclin to complete a 76-yard touchdown that tied the score at 7-7. It was the Eagles’ first meaningful offensive success against Dallas in nearly six quarters, but it did not change the direction of the game for long. The Cowboys responded with an impressive 85-yard drive, showcasing their composure. However, an apparent Philadelphia interception was overturned on replay, revealing that the ball had hit the ground, thus preserving the drive. Romo then orchestrated crucial gains by finding Jason Witten and Patrick Crayton. Tashard Choice capped off the drive with a one-yard touchdown run, giving Dallas the lead at 14-7. The Eagles were unable to recover and ultimately lost the game. The second quarter became increasingly lopsided. Crayton returned a punt 31 yards, and Romo quickly connected with Austin for 36 yards, putting Dallas in scoring range. Shaun Suisham’s 25-yard field goal gave the Cowboys a 17-7 lead. On Philadelphia’s next possession, Vick mishandled an exchange with Leonard Weaver, leading to Bobby Carpenter recovering at the Eagles’ 18-yard line. Three plays later, Romo found Austin for a six-yard touchdown, extending Dallas’s lead to 24-7. Before halftime, the Eagles gave the ball away again. Bradie James forced a fumble from Weaver and recovered it at the Philadelphia 42. Suisham converted from 48 yards as time expired, completing a 27-point second quarter and sending Dallas into halftime with a commanding 27-7 lead. In just under 14 minutes, the Cowboys had turned a tied rivalry game into a rout. Any remaining doubt vanished midway through the third quarter. Felix Jones took a handoff, burst through the right side, and outran the Philadelphia secondary for a 73-yard touchdown. This run gave Dallas a commanding 34-7 lead and solidified its status as the longest rushing touchdown in Cowboys postseason history. Jones’ performance was nothing short of spectacular, finishing the night with 148 yards on just 16 carries, impressively averaging over nine yards per attempt. The Cowboys finished with 426 total yards, including 198 on the ground, while forcing four Philadelphia turnovers. Dallas possessed the ball for more than 39 minutes and scored on five consecutive second-quarter possessions. It was not a fortunate escape or a narrow breakthrough. It was complete control of a division rival on the postseason stage. This game belongs on the countdown because it released years of pressure. The Cowboys hadn’t won a playoff game since December 1996, and every postseason failure since then had added another layer of frustration. Romo had carried the team through the 2006 snap disaster and the home defeat to the Giants in 2007. Wade Phillips had faced his own questions about winning in January. Although beating Philadelphia didn’t erase everything that followed, for one night, Dallas looked like a genuine contender and finally stopped living under the weight of its postseason drought. #Cowboys vs #Eagles 2009 Wildcard Round Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 34, Philadelphia Eagles 14 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/rO5WXQZLAb — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) August 5, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game This was the first playoff game played at Cowboys Stadium, which had opened at the beginning of the 2009 season. The announced crowd of 92,951 was, at the time, the largest attendance for an NFL postseason game outside of the Super Bowl. title: Jake Ferguson shines in second padded practice
summary: Jake Ferguson had a very productive 2025 season for the Dallas Cowboys. In fact, he had his best year overall as his 82 receptions and eigth touchdowns were both career highs, and his 600 yards were the second most most he’s produced. Unfortunately, he also had three fumbles, which gave him seven over a two-year […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - JULY 30: Jake Ferguson #87 of the Dallas Cowboys runs a route during training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields on July 30, 2026 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jake Ferguson had a very productive 2025 season for the Dallas Cowboys. In fact, he had his best year overall as his 82 receptions and eigth touchdowns were both career highs, and his 600 yards were the second most most he’s produced. Unfortunately, he also had three fumbles, which gave him seven over a two-year span, and his 7.3 per catch were a career low. Despite undoubtedly being the top tight end on the team, Ferguson came into training camp needing to show that he put his up-and-down season behind him. On Tuesday, he was one of the best performers at practice Ferguson was able to make several good plays in the passing game. One of them was a beautiful seam ball he caught in front of cornerback Shavon Revel. His biggest play of the day yardage-wise saw Ferguson turn on the jets with rookie safety Caleb Downs trailing. To top it off, Ferguson also beat safety Markquese Bell for a touchdown in the back of the end zone after a beautiful throw from Dak Prescott. SeamGod. 4 to 87. #Cowboys pic.twitter.com/sRbgOpNXaB — Patrik [No C] Walker (@VoiceOfTheStar) August 4, 2026 Jake Ferguson pic.twitter.com/F009CG8wga — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) August 4, 2026 Dak finds Jake Ferguson in the back of the end zone pic.twitter.com/ruWLRRpFFd — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) August 3, 2026 His name doesn’t get the needle moving like CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens, but Ferguson is a key element to the Cowboys’ passing game. The threat to make plays in the middle of the field helps Lamb and Pickens carve up opposing defenses and also gives Ryan Flournoy opportunities to eat. Ferguson is a chain mover as he’s racked up 95 first downs over the last three seasons. Ferguson looks more explosive so far in camp. Granted, he’s not a burner or anything, but adding a little quickness can certainly make him a bigger weapon. He’s in the second year of his four-year, $52 million deal, and after somewhat mixed results a season ago, Ferguson is looking to remind Dallas why they extended him last July.

title: 3 questions that have developed at Cowboys training camp
summary: The Dallas Cowboys have done some good things to start training camp. The stars of camp have been the usual suspects, but others have been breaking into the spotlight, especially some of the rookies. When players that you aren’t counting on to contribute immediately start showing up, it’s like finding hidden money. Yet, there are […]
full_text: May 1, 2026; Frisco, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys linebacker Malachi Lawrence (57) goes through a drill during practice at the Ford Center at the Star Training Facility in Frisco, Texas. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images The Dallas Cowboys have done some good things to start training camp. The stars of camp have been the usual suspects, but others have been breaking into the spotlight, especially some of the rookies. When players that you aren’t counting on to contribute immediately start showing up, it’s like finding hidden money. Yet, there are questions that have come up that may worry some fans and possibly even make the team break the piggy bank. Here are three questions that have cropped up so far in training camp. Do they have enough pass rush? While the back seven has made plays, especially defending the pass at training camp, the pass rush has been slow to develop. Dallas’ interior defensive line is built to stop the run, but for where the Cowboys were last year, they aren’t showing consistent ability to pressure the passer outside of blitzes. Donovan Ezeiruaku and Malachi Lawrence are young but the hope was they would ignite the pass rush. Ezeiruaku was sent out of practice today for his role in a scuffle, perhaps also some frustration on his part. Rashan Gary is a veteran in the edge rusher group, but his calling card is more akin to stopping the run. The front office has teased about getting more veteran help, but do they stoke the embers on reigniting talks regarding Las Vegas Raiders edge rusher Maxx Crosby? The Cowboys know that Crosby isn’t happy with the Raiders, and what would be the point of prolonging hanging on to a disgruntled player? The Cowboys and the Raiders have an excellent working relationship, so the two sides coming together isn’t far-fetched. Or, maybe the Cowboys stay the course, and Christian Parker finds ways to generate more pressure ahead of the preseason and joint practices with the Los Angeles Rams and New Orleans Saints. It’s not time to panic, but you couldn’t fault fans for being somewhat antsy about the defense getting to the quarterback so far. Does Dallas still need a veteran linebacker? For weeks, if not longer, the Cowboys have been connected to veteran linebackers on the market, whether that be via trade or free agency. The names Jordyn Brooks and Bobby Wagner have been thrown around. At one point, that felt like a need, but in the weeks that have passed, it seems like adding another linebacker to the mix may be more of a luxury than anything else. Everyone is raving about rookie Jaishawn Barham and justifiably so. He has been outstanding. When you look beyond him, you have DeMarvion Overshown, who seems like he is on the cusp of greatness if he can stay healthy. DeMarvion Overshown with the first big pad pop of training camp. Hits Hunter Luepke and forces a cut back from Jaydon Blue. pic.twitter.com/Zx7erQSxm0 — Joseph Hoyt (@JoeJHoyt) August 3, 2026 Luke Schoonmaker likely thought this was a walk-in TD, but Shemar James hawks him down to stop him short of the goal line. #Cowboys defense is flying around. pic.twitter.com/yam8jTpFo9 — Patrik [No C] Walker (@VoiceOfTheStar) August 3, 2026 Dee Winters is a great fit with the team and should command a starting spot to open the season. Plus, you have Shemar James in his second season. Also, don’t lose track of Justin Barron. The Cowboys have a good chunk of change tied up in the former undrafted Syracuse linebacker and have flashed the last few days. When you further assess the inside linebacker room, the need at linebacker doesn’t feel as strong as it did during the offseason. Has Jaydon Blue already taken the RB2 two job, and if so, what does that also mean? Talk about getting off to a fast start. Now in his sophomore season, Jaydon Blue looks hungry to carve out a bigger role for himself. In the early portion of training camp, he has shown to be electric with his speed and agility in the open field, breaking one big run after another. Jaydon Blue pic.twitter.com/eDJ5Iq1mG5 — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) August 4, 2026 On Tuesday, he made another explosive play as he took a short screen pass for a big gain. It’s hard to ignore just how good he has looked, which makes you think: Is the RB2 spot his to lose? Phil Mafah is doing his best to challenge for the spot, and Malik Davis hasn’t popped. While for Blue, it would be great if he, in fact, had lapped the other runners for the primary spot behind Javonte Williams, what does that also mean for the rest of the running backs on the roster? Assuming Blue is the second option, where does that leave Mafah? Has he done enough to be in serious consideration of pushing Davis, who made a few big plays himself last year? The first preseason game in less than two weeks against the Arizona Cardinals will be very telling with how much or little Blue plays and who gets the majority of the work between Mafah, Davis, and Israel Abanikanda.

title: Cowboys have groundwork for Quinnen Williams extension
summary: Stephen Jones made headlines last week when he announced the Dallas Cowboys are “absolutely” willing to start long-term contract talks with defensive tackle Quinnen Williams, who they acquired via trade from the New York Jets a little less than a year ago. Williams is currently under contract through the 2027 season, so getting an extension […]
full_text: Stephen Jones made headlines last week when he announced the Dallas Cowboys are “absolutely” willing to start long-term contract talks with defensive tackle Quinnen Williams, who they acquired via trade from the New York Jets a little less than a year ago. Cowboys EVP Stephen Jones said DT Quinnen Williams is at the top of the list of players they want to get signed long term. “Absolutely. We’re very open to that. We want Quinnen here for the long haul.” They’ve already had talks with his agent. — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) July 28, 2026 Williams is currently under contract through the 2027 season, so getting an extension done with him sooner rather than later could be in everyone’s best interest. Fortunately, Oxnard has proven to be friendly grounds for contract talks in years past and could be so once again seeing as how both parties seem to be mutually interested in sticking together long-term. Cowboys DT Quinnen Williams said Dallas is “for sure” where he wants to be long term. “I definitely want to be here for the long haul. I want to win.” pic.twitter.com/4UnJE0pj4D — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) July 29, 2026 With Williams expressing his desire to stick in Dallas long-term, and the Cowboys openness to lock him up for the foreseeable future, this deal could get done at some point before the 2026 season kicks off. That’s especially true if the organization pulls off the “substantive” trade everyone speculating about. To make such a move, they’d have to do some finagling with the salary-cap. While there are some concerns when signing any player to a big money contract, Williams’ availability/production throughout his seven-year career speaks for itself. The 29-year-old is one of the top players at his position and will end up getting paychecks by the Cowboys or someone else in the not-too-distant future. Fortunately for him and the Cowboys, the groundwork has already been laid. The recent contract extensions for Philadelphia Eagles DT Jalen Carter and Tennessee Titans DT Jeffery Simmons has laid the groundwork for the Cowboys and Williams’ representatives to potentially work something out quickly. There will of course be some going back and forth between both parties haggling to try to get the best deal possible, but that’s just part of the business. The Eagles recently signed Carter to a four-year, $152 million extension with $106 million guaranteed. The 25-year-old two-time Pro Bowler and second-team All-Pro (2024) will make an average of $38 million per year, making him the highest-paid DT in the league. $38 million per year would be the top of the market Williams’ reps could seek, but Jeffery Simmons’ recent deal is probably more realistic. Until Carter signed his recent extension, Simmons was briefly the highest-paid DT in the league receiving a three-year, $105.8 million deal with $100 million guaranteed and $35.3 million AVV. Like Williams, Simmons is also 29 years old and a seven-year pro. From a starting to a production standpoint, their careers pretty much are a mirror image of one another. Simmons and Williams are four-time Pro Bowl players and each has been named as a First-Team All-Pro in their careers. Each has about 100 starts under their belts since entering the league as first-round picks in 2019 and both have about the same QB sacks, Williams with 41.5 and Simmons with 42.5. Considering all of the similarities with Simmons (age, production, starts), the extension he received from the Titans is probably similar to what the Cowboys and Williams’ reps work out. Knowing that, it wouldn’t be a surprise at all if No. 92’s long-term future in Dallas is settled sometime soon.
