title: Cowboys news: Kenny Clark, Quinnen Williams making an impression
summary: Tyler Smith on facing ‘top tier’ DTs in practice, position clarity and more – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com Tyler Smith has enjoyed the early training camp battles with Quinnen Williams. “I feel like things are going well,” [Tyler] Smith said. “Obviously, putting on the pads is just getting back into the physicality that the football season […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - JULY 30: Quinnen Williams #92 of the Dallas Cowboys in a defensive stance during training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields on July 30, 2026 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images Tyler Smith on facing ‘top tier’ DTs in practice, position clarity and more – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com Tyler Smith has enjoyed the early training camp battles with Quinnen Williams. “I feel like things are going well,” [Tyler] Smith said. “Obviously, putting on the pads is just getting back into the physicality that the football season entails, but I feel like we’re off to a great start. Obviously, there are things to clean up, every day is not perfect, but I think we’re building towards what we’re trying to be.” That doesn’t mean it’s been easy. Facing him on the other side of the line now are Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark, two veterans who have won Pro Bowls in their career and weren’t lining up across from Smith at camp last year. They did see each other in practice during the season, but battling in Oxnard is different. “I feel like where we were at last year, I didn’t feel like we had as many live reps,” Smith said of facing Williams and Clark. “But definitely getting the training camp experience has definitely been better. I feel like it’s a whole different brand of physicality. We get way more good on good reps than we do during the season, because there’s not as much load management there. I feel like it’s really great work.” Smith’s battles with Williams have been the ones that have drawn a lot of attention from on-lookers, as the pair are both among the best players at their position. From Smith’s perspective, the two are only getting better by playing one another. “I think it’s great for me and great for him as a player,” Smith said. “I think just being able to go against somebody every day that’s going to push you to be your best and like, there is going to be times when you win. There’s going to be times when you lose. But ultimately what are you learning form that rep? What are you learning from those experiences? And that’s something even in year five, and he’s [year eight], that’s something that we’re both learning and both going through.” ‘Bash Brothers’ Quinnen Williams, Kenny Clark are setting the tone at Cowboys training camp – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News The Dallas Cowboys might have the best defensive tackle duo in the NFL. The first practice of training camp is not supposed to be physical. League rules even try to limit the physicality when the pads come on, let alone when they aren’t worn early. It’s hard to limit the inherent physicality of defensive tackles like Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark, however. Just ask starting center Cooper Beebe. “The first couple of days, when you go against those dudes and, boom, you get a long arm to the chest with no pads, it definitely left some bruises for sure,” Beebe said. Bruises will heal, but the benefits of working with two defensive tackles like Williams and Clark — the Bash Brothers for this Cowboys defensive line — should sustain. At least the Cowboys hope so. The Cowboys have trumpeted the importance of Williams and Clark — two additions that weren’t here at training camp last year — to the team’s defense. The two have provided added benefits for the team’s offense, as well. Especially on the interior. “They’re heavy in the middle,” Cowboys left guard Tyler Smith said, “and you know when you go against them you have to come with your business.” That’s been evident in the first five days of practice. That’s especially true when you compare it to years past. Last year, the Cowboys had a defensive tackle group of former first-round pick Mazi Smith, veteran Solomon Thomas, Perrion Winfrey — a spring league standout who ultimately made the team — seventh-round pick Jay Toia and Osa Odighizuwa. Only Toia remains on the roster. This year, the starting offensive line has mostly faced Williams, Clark, free agent acquisition Otito Ogbonnia and veteran Jonathan Bullard. Two Cowboys starters limited in Tuesday’s practice; Ezeiruaku ejected for punch – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram The hype around Jaishawn Barham continues to build in DeMarvion Overshown’s absence. In Tuesday’s training camp practice for the Dallas Cowboys, linebacker DeMarvion Overshown and offensive tackle Tyler Guyton were limited while dealing with soreness. Overshown had a lower body/leg issue while Guyton nursed elbow discomfort. Neither injury is considered concerning, but the team will manage the workload of each player as camp ramps up in the coming days. Also in Tuesday’s practice, outside linebacker Donovan Ezeiruaku was ejected for throwing a punch at offensive tackle Terence Steele. Per head coach Brian Schottenheimer’s policy, Ezeiruaku was thrown out of practice, as he was escorted out by a member of the front office. In Overshown’s absence during the team period on Tuesday, Dee Winters and Jaishawn Barham were featured as the starting linebackers with the first-team unit, while Nate Thomas filled in for Guyton’s absence. It came just a few minutes after Schottenheimer had mentioned that Guyton would maintain his spot as the starting left tackle after Thomas’ slow start to training camp in what has been pinned as a position battle between the two players heading into Oxnard. Each player was slated to get a four-day rotation as the starter, but Guyton remains in place after the first four days. “We talked to Nate and said that he needs to show us a little more consistent play to push for that. I know we had told you guys about the rotation,” Schottenheimer said. “Tyler will stay at left tackle. I’m excited to see how Nate handles that challenge, but Tyler is playing really, really well.” Barham stepping in for Overshown is yet another feather in the rookie third-round pick’s cap early in training camp, as he has stacked together multiple strong practice performances. “His ability to apply the things we’re coaching,” Schottenheimer said about what has stood out about Barham. “We’ve put him in some different spots, which is really cool. You see and know the physicality, but to know and apply it has been great.” Packers’ Micah Parsons: Playing vs. Cowboys in Week 6 ‘realistic’ – Rob Demovsky, ESPN.com When the schedule came out, it seemed inevitable Micah Parsons’ first game back would be against the Cowboys. For a guy who said he’s not into timelines but rather coming back as strong as possible, Micah Parsons sounded optimistic about one thing: He likes his chances of playing in the Green Bay Packers ‘ Week 6 game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lambeau Field. “I think it’s very realistic,” Parsons said Tuesday. He acknowledged, however, that there’s still work to be done in his rehab from last year’s torn ACL/meniscus injury sustained in Week 15. “I wouldn’t say it’s not possible, but, at the same time, in these next 10 weeks — 10, 12 weeks from now on — we’ve got to do our part to make it possible,” Parsons said in his first session with reporters since training camp opened last week. “It’s not off the board, but we’ve got to put the work in.” Parsons opened training camp on the physically unable to perform list and likely will remain with that designation when the regular season opens. That means he would miss at least the first four games of the season. However, a change in the PUP rule now allows players to begin practicing after just two regular-season weeks. In the past, players could not do so for the first four weeks of the season. Given that the Packers rarely allow players coming off ACL injuries to practice earlier than nine months after surgery, Parsons isn’t likely to practice until late September. The Packers play the Chicago Bears in Week 5 (Oct. 4), followed by the Cowboys (Oct. 11). The Packers were 9-3-1 when Parsons went down against the Denver Broncos , and they didn’t win another game the rest of the way. Parsons had 12.5 sacks and,…

title: Jonah Coleman is turning heads, and Sean Payton is taking notice
summary: Few aspects of the Denver Broncos training camp top the risers and fallers. Everyone knows the players who have their spots on the roster scribbled in ink. But it’s the players who are fighting for a spot or clawing their way up the depth chart that creates the best storylines. That’s especially true for rookies. […]
full_text: CENTENNIAL , CO - JUNE 16: Jonah Coleman (20) of the Denver Broncos works out during minicamp at the Broncos Park in Centennial, Colorado on Tuesday, June 16, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images Few aspects of the Denver Broncos training camp top the risers and fallers. Everyone knows the players who have their spots on the roster scribbled in ink. But it’s the players who are fighting for a spot or clawing their way up the depth chart that creates the best storylines. That’s especially true for rookies. After Broncos practice on Wednesday, Sean Payton was asked if there has been a pleasant surprise at this point. “Fair question. I think the young runner, you don’t feel a rookie with (running back) Jonah (Coleman). He’s playing. It’s been harder with some of the linemen because we haven’t been in pads in fairness to them. Then a couple of these young linebackers, we’re getting to see them move around, make the calls. There’s a lot to that position, a lot of it is key and diagnose. That’s been good.” The fact that Payton singled out Coleman is no doubt a positive sign (thanks, John Madden). When Denver selected the running back out of Washington in the fourth round, the pick was widely celebrated. Adding his running style and abilities to this offense gives the running back room another element and a different running style. Now Coleman is getting praise from Payton as a pleasant surprise at this point in training camp. But the compliments from Payton on Wednesday didn’t stop there. He was also asked about second-year receiver Pat Bryant and what area he’s progressed the most in since last year. “(I’m) really pleased with how he’s doing,” Payton said to the media on Wednesday. “He’s just one of those congested ball catchers. His feet stay on the ground. So when receivers catch the ball with their feet on the ground, they’re usually pretty good run after the catch. You don’t see him skipping in the air or jumping. That means he has a lot of confidence in catching this thing the right way. “I think in college in that final year (at Illinois), I think he had three walk-off touchdowns. Like literally last play of the game in-cuts where he caught it and didn’t … He was full stride when he caught it. If you’re breaking stride for a catch, there’s that tick of a second everyone gets a little bit of leverage on you. He’s extremely smart. He’s doing really well.” We all know the players who are projected to make the biggest impact for the Broncos this season. Seeing the younger players shine at this point is what will make the team better.

title: 2026 Denver Broncos Training Camp: Day 5 News and Notes
summary: Today was one of the more important practices of training camp. It was another fully padded practice, but the intensity was ramped up, and they had their longest practice session thus far. Unfortunately, for the third straight day, another Broncos starter left practice early with an injury, and today it was wide receiver Jaylen Waddle. […]
full_text: CENTENNIAL , CO - AUGUST 5: J.K. Dobbins (27) of the Denver Broncos works out with teammates during training camp at Broncos Park in Centennial, Colorado on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images Today was one of the more important practices of training camp. It was another fully padded practice, but the intensity was ramped up, and they had their longest practice session thus far. Unfortunately, for the third straight day, another Broncos starter left practice early with an injury, and today it was wide receiver Jaylen Waddle. Thankfully, like Wattenberg and Bonitto, it seems like he avoided anything significant, but he was absent for most of the practice. Same with Courtland Sutton, who received back-to-back veteran rest days, so the Broncos offense was down their top two targets. #BroncosCamp work zone 🚧 pic.twitter.com/rzBrjb6FnR — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) August 5, 2026 For the third straight padded practice, the Denver Broncos defense, specifically their defensive line/ front 7, dominated the practice. DJ Jones, Malcolm Roach, Jonathon Cooper, Uwazurike, and the rest simply created havoc all practice. Sam Ehlinger took QB2 reps again today and looked good, but Payton said there’s no official competition happening there, and we have updates on select players from Sean Payton. Plus, as always, news and notes, injury updates, tweets from camp, quotes, and more! Defense and front 7 win again The offense started camp hot and had fans and media excited because we haven’t seen an offense come out firing like this in a long time in training camp. Well, that excitement was short-lived, because when the pads came on, the Denver Broncos front 7 came alive. Today it was Malcolm Roach, Jonathon Cooper, DJ Jones, and Uwazurike just absolutely dominating the Denver Broncos offensive line and limiting their overall production. It didn’t help that the offense did not have Waddle, Sutton, Wattenberg, and at times, McGlinchey and Powers, but still, the defense dominated. Roach, Jones, Uwazurike, and the rest of the Denver Broncos defensive line dominated the run game and were also able to get after the quarterbacks. It was a strong performance from three players who will be very important to the success of this team this upcoming season and potentially replacing John Franklin-Myers in this defense. "We've tasted it, now it's time to cook the meal, eat it, and take a break… we're about to eat again, it's time!" DJ Jones on the Denver Broncos' defense HUNGER going into this season 🔥 pic.twitter.com/rKdvLBFiru — DNVR Broncos (@DNVR_Broncos) August 5, 2026 Speaking of replacing JFM, veteran starting nose tackle DJ Jones believes the competition is already over and thinks Malcolm Roach will run away with the job, and that would make sense. Roach earned the contract extension from the Broncos last season while also flashing his pass rush upside. So, we could see Roach take over that JFM role, but there are a number of other defensive linemen on this team pushing for those reps. Given that depth, Jones believes the Broncos can break the NFL team sack record. He told reporters, We got what it takes and “We’ve tasted it, and now it’s time to cook the meal, eat it, and take a break”. He added, “We about to eat again” and that they have the numbers, the men, the willpower and the freewill to go out and do that, and he believes they will. The Broncos pass rush, even without John Franklin-Myers, is deep. Upfront they have Zach Allen, Malcolm Roach, the ascending Eyioma Uwazurike, Sai’vion Jones, rookie Tyler Onyedim, Jordan Jackson, Matt Henningsen, and on the edges you have Bonitto, Cooper, Elliss, Robinson, Tillman, Sanders and so on. The sack potential on this team is immense, and they should lead the NFL in sacks once again and push for that team sack record. Speaking of Uwazurike, he appears to be taking that next step in his career and becoming a problem for offensive linemen. Uwazurike taking that next step? After a not-so-great rookie year followed by a year-long suspension, it appeared Eyioma Uwazurike’s tenure with the Broncos and potentially even his football career could be over. However, he returned in 2024 and not only saved his career, but he became a key rotational player for this top-ranked Denver Broncos defense. Now, he’s looking at taking that next step and becoming a dominant defensive lineman and someone the team could count on to replace the role and snaps John Franklin Myers had wiith this team the past few seasons. "Speaking of Enyi, he can't be blocked… he's scary" 🔥 DJ Jones has some BIG praises for Eyioma Uwazurike 👀 pic.twitter.com/SIjKdEO8Xf — DNVR Broncos (@DNVR_Broncos) August 5, 2026 Jones was asked about Uwazurike’s development; he told reporters that Enyi “cannot be blocked”, he can play every position, and that “he’s scary”. “His hands and his eyes. This game is fast. It’s physical, which he has. But if you don’t have good eyes on the [defensive] line, then you’ll be lost. The leap he’s taking right now is pretty scary. Like I said, he can play every position, very physical and his eyes are 10 out of 10 now.” Head Coach Sean Payton also had high praise for the Broncos’ massive defensive lineman. He told reporters that he is proud of Enyi for bouncing back from his year-long suspension, knowing that it can end players’ careers. He also added that he has developed; he’s strong, big, and having a really good start to camp. “I’m proud of him because, you guys know this, in our sport, any sport really to just be out for a year can be difficult. He’s really come back, developed. He’s strong, he’s big and he’s having a real good start to camp. So I think you have to look at it as one less year than what’s listed because of the year out. Yes, he’s doing really well.” There’s a lot to like about Uwazurike, especially if he’s putting his entire game together. First, he’s listed at 6’6, 320 pounds (and he might be bigger than that), he’s athletic (played edge rusher at Iowa State), and he can play every position, as Jones stated and apparently cannot be blocked. If Enyi can turn into a really good player on top of the rest of the Broncos defensive line depth, this front seven could be even more dangerous and disruptive than they were last season. Updates on select players Sean Payton spoke about several players after today’s practice, so I decided to lump them all together here and give you all the updates in one place. HC Sean Payton on CB Kris Abrams-Draine “One thing about him is he’s smart. We felt that right away his rookie year. He’s one of those players, the ball kind of finds him too with his instincts. I would say he has tremendous hands. So he’s gotten stronger since his first year. He has real good key and diagnose, and a lot of traits that with his ball skills that serve him well at corner.” HC Sean Payton on EDGE Que Robinson “There were certain traits you saw on film. He’s a real good technician, and he’s one of those guys that we know has been coached hard. We felt coming into this defense from what he was playing in, there were some similarities to what we were going to ask him to do. I think that’s a help.” “I think it’s going well. He’s certainly competing for those reps in the line of scrimmage. I think it’s going really well, and again, we’ve had pads on for two days now.” HC Sean Payton on WR Lil’Jordan Humphrey “Good. It’s unusual for someone his age. We do all the metrics and they wear the chips, but his weight’s down. His movement on the field, acceleration, top-end speed is higher last season and now than it was when he was here earlier. They’re able to measure that with the Catapult. So he’s extremely smart, that’s probably one of his superpowers. He can play all three positions, and he’s a big target. HC Sean Payton on rookie TE Justin Joly “Yes, he’s coming. It’s a big jump for all those young tight ends. He’s certainly someone we feel like is better with…

title: Jaylen Waddle embracing a team-first mindset early on with the Broncos
summary: The biggest addition the Denver Broncos made this offseason was trading for wide receiver Jaylen Waddle. It came at a hefty cost. Nevertheless, the Broncos are confident they will see an immediate return on their big-time investment. Denver’s ultimate goal this season is the Super Bowl. Few teams can realistically say that, but for them—it’s […]
full_text: CENTENNIAL , CO - JULY 31: Wide receiver Jaylen Waddle (17) of the Denver Broncos sign autographs for young fans after practice on Friday, July 31, 2026, at Broncos Park in Centennial, Colo.(Photo by Timothy Hurst/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images) | Denver Post via Getty Images The biggest addition the Denver Broncos made this offseason was trading for wide receiver Jaylen Waddle. It came at a hefty cost. Nevertheless, the Broncos are confident they will see an immediate return on their big-time investment. Denver’s ultimate goal this season is the Super Bowl. Few teams can realistically say that, but for them—it’s true. In order to accomplish that, the team will have to be much better on offense and unleash untapped dimensions of their aerial attack in 2026 that were missing last year. Throughout the offseason, Waddle has earned praise from his coaches and teammates for what he brings to the table. However, he knows it will take more than just him to get the Broncos’ offense to the next level. After yesterday’s practice, Waddle approached the aforementioned with humility and embraced a team-first attitude when asked about making the offense more dynamic. “I wouldn’t even say it’s just me. We have a lot of playmakers around us, so they want to get playmakers in space. They want us to get the ball in a hurry, get the ball out fast and just allow us to create plays. I don’t necessarily think it’s just me. We have a lot of playmakers, so just designing different things to get us in space,” added Waddle. SI's @AlbertBreer on Waddle and Mims: "Jaylen Waddle has arrived as advertised. The most noticeable and unique quality he brings to the table from Miami is his combination of elite long speed and sudden stop-and-start ability." "And Marvin Mims Jr. has had an outstanding… pic.twitter.com/8S7lTxM4Xu — SleeperBroncos (@SleeperBroncos) August 4, 2026 Transitioning to a new team isn’t always easy. Though for Waddle, heading from Miami to Denver has been a relatively smooth process. While he is still learning the ropes and getting acclimated to the area, the sixth-year pro gave rave reviews about the team’s culture. Moreover, expressed gratitude for how everyone in the organization treated him from the day he arrived in the Mile High City. “It’s just the team. They welcomed me with open arms since Day 1. I kind of grew to know not just Pat, but my receiver group, and the defense and everyone. It’s like a big family here. It just makes it easy to come to work. It makes it easy to come to work, go out there and compete in front of the fans on days like this.” In his first three years in the NFL, Waddle surpassed the 1,000-yard mark. The past two seasons, there has been some statistical regression. That’s by no fault of his own and can mostly be attributed to the quarterback issues with the Dolphins. In his first year with the Broncos, the sky is the limit for Waddle. He expressed confidence and optimism for the upcoming season. One of those reasons is because of who he is going up against on a daily basis. The Broncos boast one of the league’s best secondaries that will present him with more challenges leading up to the start of the season. Iron sharpens iron, and Waddle believes going up against Denver’s high-caliber defense will improve his play. “Our defense is definitely top in the league. Just having that back and forth with them, front to the back end, to the linebackers. It just makes us play true. We try to go out there, give them good looks and compete really hard against them. Our defense is hard to get a yard on, I can tell you that.”

title: Zach Allen has become one of the Broncos’ best players
summary: Back during the 2023 offseason, the Denver Broncos made a big change on their defensive line. Dre’Mont Jones, whom many considered to be a rising star, inked a lucrative deal with the Seattle Seahawks. Subsequently, the Broncos signed Zach Allen, reuniting him with Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph. When it happened, many fans across Broncos Country […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - NOVEMBER 06: Zach Allen #99 of the Denver Broncos looks on from the field after an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Empower Field at Mile High on November 6, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Back during the 2023 offseason, the Denver Broncos made a big change on their defensive line. Dre’Mont Jones, whom many considered to be a rising star, inked a lucrative deal with the Seattle Seahawks. Subsequently, the Broncos signed Zach Allen, reuniting him with Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph. When it happened, many fans across Broncos Country were puzzled by the decision. Fast forward several years later and there’s no doubt the franchise’s leadership made the right call. Since his arrival in the Denver, Allen has been a difference maker for the team and a two-time All-Pro. Meanwhile, Jones has now moved on to his fourth different franchise since leaving the Mile High City. Yesterday, Head Coach Sean Payton fielded a variety of questions, but spent some time highlighting what makes the eighth-year pro such a great player. “He has tremendous stamina, so play 38 looks like eight, play 60 still looks like eight. So that’s a big asset at a position where it’s hard. Then I would say his intelligence and his quickness off the ball. He’ll win usually in the first second and a half of a rush, or he’ll win early. So that’s what makes him difficult,” stated Payton. In three seasons with the Broncos, Allen has only missed one game and has 50 starts. He has racked up 159 tackles, 27 tackles for loss, and 20.5 sacks. Even better? He has really upped his pass rushing prowess—with an astounding 111 quarterback hits and 159 pressures credited to his name. His presence on the Broncos’ defensive front has transformed them from an area of weakness to one of the best trench groups in the NFL. When asked whether or not there was a next step for Allen to take Payton wasn’t sure. However, he offered a simple recipe to ensure he keeps playing good football. “He’s playing at a very high level. He keeps himself in shape, and it’s hard to play that position, the snaps he plays. We have to be careful, I’ve said this before, of making sure that we’re rotating him and that he’s not out there too long,” added Payton. In 2023, Allen played 911 snaps (81-percent) and an astounding 964 snaps (89-precent) in 2024. Last season, the Broncos carried an extra defensive lineman and rotated their front a bit more. For the 2025 season, Allen saw 797 snaps (71-percent) and was still incredibly productive. Even with less snaps, he was just as productive, if not more, in a lot of statistical categories than seasons prior. Last August, the Broncos rewarded Allen with a four-year contract extension worth up to over $102 million dollars. As his career continues, the former Boston College standout keeps getting better with age and experience. With virtuall “There are always things to improve on. That’s the really cool thing about this group is that we’re just constantly trying to find new ways to get better. It all starts with ‘VJ’. He sets such a high standard. Yes, we were good last year, but there were still a lot of things that we could have been better at and cleaned up,” remarked Allen. The Broncos defense led the league in quarterback sacks last season and also ranked high in various other categories. Though one key area for improvement would be forcing more turnovers. On top of that, minimizing penalties on that side of the ball, which extended drives for the opposition. As far as Allen is concerned, this year’s defense has all the potential to be better than what we have seen the prior two seasons. It will take a little bit of hard work and dedication, but that’s something he and his teammates are looking forward to accomplishing. “I just want to keep building off of that. There is a saying that you can never stay the same, you are always getting better or getting worse. I’m just always trying to get better every day.”

title: Sai’vion Jones looking to fill some big shoes
summary: There is talk coming out of training camp about Sai’vion Jones being ready to take a big step forward in Vance Joseph’s defense this season. Veteran defensive lineman Zach Allen had high praise for Jones the other day, mentioning he has taken a big leap entering his second season. With the loss of Johnathan Franklin-Myers […]
full_text: There is talk coming out of training camp about Sai’vion Jones being ready to take a big step forward in Vance Joseph’s defense this season. Veteran defensive lineman Zach Allen had high praise for Jones the other day, mentioning he has taken a big leap entering his second season. With the loss of Johnathan Franklin-Myers to the Tennessee Titans in free agency, a large void in the defensive front to the tune of roughly 500 snaps across from Allen. It is worth noting that the Denver Broncos defense under Vance Joseph typically uses a fairly heavy rotation of five players along their standard three-man line. During his rookie season, Jones didn’t see the field much. That isn’t unusual for mid-round defensive lineman. It’s a big jump from college to the pros. He saw playing time in Week 4, 14, and 18 with just 33 total defensive snaps. Which means for those of us eye-test guys, there isn’t a lot to go on from his rookie season. At this point, it’s all a projection. I’m excited to see what Jones will be able to accomplish this season. He’s darn near a clone in size to Zach Allen, with both of them being 6’5” and 285 pounds. The third-round pick from the 2025 NFL Draft has had a year to study this defense, get his feet wet, and learn from one of the best-coached defensive fronts in the game today. The sky is the limit for this young Bronco. title: Discussion: What’s the proper concern level for Jahmyr Gibbs’ hold-in?
summary: Jahmyr Gibbs’ hold-in for a new contract officially enters Week 2 on Thursday, as the Detroit Lions will participate in their seventh training camp practice this offseason. Thus far, there have been no tangible signs of progress between the Lions and Gibbs, but there haven’t been any reports of stagnation or sticking points with negotiations, […]
full_text: Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs (0) on field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday, August 3, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Jahmyr Gibbs’ hold-in for a new contract officially enters Week 2 on Thursday, as the Detroit Lions will participate in their seventh training camp practice this offseason. Thus far, there have been no tangible signs of progress between the Lions and Gibbs, but there haven’t been any reports of stagnation or sticking points with negotiations, either. Really, all the evidence we have about negotiations are the scant details we’re getting from the team itself. Both Lions coach Dan Campbell and general manager Brad Holmes have expressed public interest in getting a deal done, and on Wednesday, Holmes said they are engaged in talks. So this isn’t a situation in which the Lions are refusing to pay Gibbs or closed to any talks. However, there have been a few signs that are relatively discouraging. A week ago, Campbell said he “wasn’t sweating” Gibbs’ hold-in, but he also admitted he was surprised the contract hasn’t been finalized yet. “I thought we’d have been done by now,” Campbell said. On Wednesday, Holmes told SiriusXM they’re “having dialogue” with Gibbs , but his body language did not scream optimistic, and when reassured by the radio host that it’ll get done, his response was an uninspiring “that’s the hope.” So today’s Question of the Day is: What’s your concern level regarding Jahmyr Gibbs’ hold-in? My answer: I’m still pretty low. Let’s call it a 2/10 total. Admittedly, we’re entering uncharted territory with the Lions. Any time they’ve publicly expressed an interest in extending a player, they’ve been able to do so in a very timely manner. So, on the surface, it’s a bit concerning that’s not how negotiations are going this time around. Additionally, I figured as soon as Bijan Robinson signed his three-year extension with the Atlanta Falcons, that Gibbs’ deal would come about almost immediately. It’s been around 48 hours since, and all has been quiet. That all being said, I’m still not that concerned. We’re still very early in training camp, and while I’d certainly like Gibbs to be out there in a new offense with a new offensive line, there is more than enough time for him to enter the picture and be ready by Week 1. I trust that Gibbs’ appearance at practices is a sign of good faith and no ill-will, and I do expect the Robinson deal to move things along relatively quickly. And with Campbell’s mostly-optimistic comments on the situation, I’m assuming things will be just fine. Simply put, if Campbell isn’t sweating it, there’s no reason I should be. That said, if we’re beyond the first preseason game and Gibbs is still sidelined, that’s when the worry starts to creep up into the 4-6 range, and if we’re nearing the end of preseason, that’s when I’d jump to a 8-10. But, for now, it’s early. It’s okay to be patient here. What is your concern level for the Jahmyr Gibbs contract negotiations? title: Detroit Lions veteran TE to return from injury
summary: According to the NFL transaction wire, veteran tight end Tyler Conklin has passed his physical after missing the first week of training camp with a calf injury suffered in the spring. That almost certainly means Conklin will come off the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list when the Lions return to practice on Thursday. His […]
full_text: Detroit Lions tight end Tyler Conklin (83) practices a drill during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co According to the NFL transaction wire, veteran tight end Tyler Conklin has passed his physical after missing the first week of training camp with a calf injury suffered in the spring. That almost certainly means Conklin will come off the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list when the Lions return to practice on Thursday. His return comes just in time, as the Lions’ tight end room has suffered several injuries already in camp. Veteran tight end Anthony Firkser has already been placed on injured reserve with a broken leg. And the Lions also placed Miles Kitselman on injured reserve with a leg injury of his own. To help out, Detroit has added Nick Muse and re-signed Zach Horton. But the return of Conklin figures to be the biggest impact of all the Lions’ maneuvering in the tight end room. Conklin is an eight-year veteran who has put up at least 400 receiving yards on four different occasions. Detroit signed him to a one-year, $1.3 million deal this offseason to compete for the tight end depth behind Sam LaPorta and Brock Wright. Though Conklin is coming off a tough year with the Chargers, he caught at least 50 passes in each of the four previous seasons. He brings a strong blend of receiving skills and physical play to a room that struggled with its depth last season. Additionally, the Lions re-signed wide receiver Tarik Black to fill the roster spot left after placing Kitselman on injured reserve. And receiver Lawrence Keys reverted to the Lions’ injured reserve after the team waived him with an injury designation earlier in the week.

title: Detroit Lions announce new president, CEO Richard Haddad
summary: The Detroit Lions announced on Wednesday they’ve hired a new team president and CEO, and he doesn’t have to move too far for work. The new team president is Richard Haddad, a Michigan native who has served as the Chief Operating Officer and Chief Legal Officer of the Detroit Pistons since January of 2022. Prior […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 05: A detailed view of the Detroit Lions logo on a helmet on the field before the game against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on December 05, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions announced on Wednesday they’ve hired a new team president and CEO, and he doesn’t have to move too far for work. The new team president is Richard Haddad, a Michigan native who has served as the Chief Operating Officer and Chief Legal Officer of the Detroit Pistons since January of 2022. Prior to that, he served as the Executive Vice President of business affairs/administration and general counsel for the Pistons. “Rich is a proven leader who understands what it means to steward an iconic sports franchise in the city of Detroit, and we are thrilled that he is bringing that experience to the Lions,” Sheila Hamp said in a written statement. “Throughout our process, Rich’s experience, steady leadership style, and grasp on the present and future state of team sports were clear differentiators. My family and I are excited to work with Rich on driving the Lions forward in our continued pursuit to bring a championship to Detroit.” Haddad made Sports Business Journal’s “Forty Under 40” list in 2022 . Here’s what he had to say to the publication back then: “Detroit declared bankruptcy within a year and a half of my moving here, which is probably the bottom,” Haddad said. “It’s been incredible over the few years since then to see the city’s resurgence, and to have the opportunity through the Pistons to try to play a small role in accelerating all that.” In addition to his work with the Pistons, he was part of the effort to bring back a WNBA team to Detroit ( currently scheduled for 2029 ), “I am thrilled to join the Detroit Lions organization as its next President and CEO,” Haddad said via a press release. “I want to thank Sheila Hamp and the Ford family for their trust in me, along with Tom Gores and Arn Tellem for 14 great years with the Pistons. As a lifelong Lions fan, I understand firsthand how much this team means to this city and state, and I’m honored and humbled to lead this franchise. Sheila, Rod [Wood], Brad [Holmes] and Dan [Campbell] have built an incredible foundation, and I can’t wait to work with them to build on that and deliver for our fans and our community.” Haddad replaces Rod Wood, who announced he was retiring earlier this offseason. Per the Lions’ official story on the hire, Wood, Hamp, Bill Ford, Chris Spielman, and Lindsay Verstegen were involved with the hiring, along with the advisory firm Russell Reynolds. Wood will remain in place until Haddad completes his work with the Pistons and his transfer to the Lions is complete. Haddad is expected to take over in early September.

title: Why the Detroit Lions made a key change to the 1st padded practice
summary: As the Detroit Lions transitioned from individual drills to team drills on Monday—the first training camp practice with full pads—a familiar scene arrived. On the far field, the players amassed in a semicircle around coach Dan Campbell. Training camp veterans and keen-eyed witnesses knew what was coming next. It’s the very same thing that has […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MICHIGAN - JULY 29: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions and head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions laugh during Detroit Lions Training Camp at Detroit Lions Meijer Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the Detroit Lions transitioned from individual drills to team drills on Monday—the first training camp practice with full pads—a familiar scene arrived. On the far field, the players amassed in a semicircle around coach Dan Campbell. Training camp veterans and keen-eyed witnesses knew what was coming next. It’s the very same thing that has kicked off the first padded practice every year under Campbell: one-on-one tackling. Reporters scrambled to the end zone of the far field to ensure they didn’t miss a single one of these highly entertaining reps. However, what they saw was something different than in previous years. Campbell has previously set the tone of padded practices by going full live tackling during these drills, meaning the defenders would attempt legitimate tackles all the way to the ground. Not every team likes to do this, but in Campbell’s passionate speech on “Hard Knocks” in 2022 , he explained why he thought it was important. “I had a couple of you look at me like ‘What the (expletive)? Why are we going live (tackling)?’ I got it. Here’s what I need, man. I need you to trust me. I swear to god I’m not a lunatic. I swear to you. If I absolutely knew we could get to where we need to get without ever putting pads on, I would do it. I swear to you. But also for us as a team to get better defensively, what is the essence of what we do? What are the two things? Pursuit and tackle. Pursuit and tackle. Man, if you don’t work on tackling, if we don’t work on run after the catch, making a move, man, what are we doing? Then we finally get to Week 8 and we come to life because we’ve got enough reps? That’s why I’m doing it. I swear, man, I don’t want to put anybody in jeopardy, but we have to do it, man. I believe it.” But on Monday, the Lions didn’t do live tackling. Instead, they opted to do two-hand touch to start padded practices, a pretty significant shift in strategy. On Tuesday, I asked him why the change. “Let’s just do it to where these guys get a feel,” Campbell said. “It’s crazy how you saw that drill under control and all this.” His argument, essentially, was that when you go live tackling—particularly that early in camp—the form is sloppy and dangerous. Players excited by the promise of contact try to run over each other—which is forbidden in this drill, even when it’s live. But by easing them in, the form gets settled before the actual tackling gets done. “Let’s just fundamentally, let’s go through it a couple times,” Campbell said. Campbell found another benefit of two-hand touch drills. In previous years, he had held some players out of that drill to protect them. But now those players can participate and show off the one-cut skills they have, which also helps the defender. “There were some guys I held out of that drill last year. And that are—they have got some juice, and they got some cuts, and they got some—,” Campbell said. “So, by not doing it live, you get them and keep them in the drill, which works the tackler a little bit.” This is just one of many changes the Lions have made to their approach this offseason. They switched around their spring OTA and minicamp schedule, opted not to do joint practices, and it sounds like they intend to play some starters in the preseason, as well. But don’t mistake Monday’s practice as a scrapping of live tackling completely. “We will get to that drill and do it live for you, Jeremy,” Campbell said. “It is coming, my friend. I’m telling you.”

For Pride of Detroit, we are tasked with fielding questions from Detroit Lions fans, and this week’s question asks fans to look ahead to the Lions’ first preseason game: an August 13th, Thursday night matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals. The Lions have made it known that they are getting back to basics this offseason, and we’ve seen that play out through the first week of training camp. With the Lions’ preseason matchup with the Bengals just over one week away, it’s fair to wonder if they’ll continue this trend of returning to traditional methods, specifically with playing their starters in the preseason. For the past several years, the Lions have participated in joint practices and have deemed that exposure enough for their starters to rest during their preseason games. However, with this return-to-basics approach and no joint practices on the docket, could we see the starters play in the preseason, and if so, how much should they play? At the start of training camp, coach Dan Campbell was asked about this topic, and he was non-committal with his response, indicating he would need more time to see where the team was at: “I would like to, but there again, this thing moves as we get through these practices. What do we look like? Who needs work? Do they need to play together? Are there players that aren’t getting enough intensity in practice? And the only way to get them there is they have to play preseason games or we got to go live. So, we’ll work around that stuff. Right now I would like to, but we’ll see how it goes.” While a lot has changed over the past week, it’s still unclear how Campbell’s perspective has changed. But we also want to know what fans think on this topic. Should the Lions play their starters? How much would you prefer? How much is too much? summary: The Green Bay Packers’ players won’t have another open practice until after Friday’s Family Night scrimmage at Lambeau Field, but the media did get a chance to talk to the team’s coordinators on Wednesday. For the first time during training camp, we got to hear feedback from each unit’s top coaches, rather than just from […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 13: Head coach Jonathan Gannon reacts to an officials call during a game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on October 13, 2024 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. The Packers defeated the Cardinals 34-13. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ players won’t have another open practice until after Friday’s Family Night scrimmage at Lambeau Field, but the media did get a chance to talk to the team’s coordinators on Wednesday. For the first time during training camp, we got to hear feedback from each unit’s top coaches, rather than just from head coach Matt LaFleur. Here’s your recap of the major news from today’s press conferences. Cam Achord, special teams First-year Packers special teams coordinator Cam Achord was asked how Trey Smack likes his kicks to be held. He then came off the podium and did this for almost two minutes. Enjoy. pic.twitter.com/sD6yhBbZDB — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) August 5, 2026 I’m not going to bore you guys with too much special teams talk, but Cam Achord’s breakdown of why Trey Smack prefers a different way for his holder to position the ball than the typical straight up and down every single time is worth your time. Inject this into my veins. More of this PLEASE. Jonathan Gannon, defense So far, the Packers, overall, have exceeded expectations, according to new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon. This goes for “leadership, the operation and players,” in Gannon’s words. That’s great to hear! Gannon brought up versatility a lot, in the context of almost any position group in his unit. The interior defensive linemen are playing everywhere right now. The edge rushers are even kicking inside. The safeties are being placed all over the field. He said that they have the talent in the secondary to present different looks to get into the same calls, because Xavier McKinney, Evan Williams and Javon Bullard can do so much. As far as what his defense will look like, Gannon said that “each game should look different,” not because of the Packers’ talent but because of the variance from opposing offenses from week to week. It’ll be interesting to monitor how many tools Gannon has in the toolbox early on in the season, when Green Bay doesn’t have Micah Parsons, and how that will change as his players get more time in the system and Parsons returns. Adam Stenavich, offense Offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich seemed pretty pleased with his unit, stating that backup interior offensive linemen Jager Burton (a fifth-round rookie) and Jacob Monk (a third-year fifth-round pick) have the “right mindset.” He also stated that Jordan Morgan is “our left tackle, and he’s out there to prove it to everybody,” if anyone had any questions about whether or not Morgan was going to stick outside after primarily playing guard for his first two years in the NFL. Stenavich called left tackle Morgan’s “natural spot.” On the tight end front, with all the injuries, Josh Whyle and Drake Dabney have been forced into the lineup with the starting offense a lot during camp. Stenavich stated that both have improved and that maybe no one has “improved as much as [Dabney] in the first few days.” He also called Dabney more of an in-line tight end than Whyle, who has been playing a lot of fullback in camp, though that might just be the nature of being down so many bodies at the position. Running back MarShawn Lloyd, who has only been healthy enough to play 10 regular-season snaps over two seasons after being taken in the third round, has been looking good in camp, per Steno. He’s hoping that Lloyd gets a big workload in the preseason, considering how many limited live snaps Lloyd has gotten in NFL games for a third-year player.

title: Who is Anthony Campbell? Packers newcomer making his mark
summary: In an unsettled defensive line room, an unheralded newcomer is making his mark. Anthony Campbell, a 6-foot-6, 307-pound prospect who’s spent his still-young career on the fringes of the NFL, has thrown his name in the ring as a contender for the Packers’ 53-man roster. As Javon Hargrave and Devonte Wyatt come along slowly in […]
full_text: Anthony Campbell #60 and Jaden Crumedy #63 of the Green Bay Packers greet fans while walking to practice at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images In an unsettled defensive line room, an unheralded newcomer is making his mark. Anthony Campbell, a 6-foot-6, 307-pound prospect who’s spent his still-young career on the fringes of the NFL, has thrown his name in the ring as a contender for the Packers’ 53-man roster. As Javon Hargrave and Devonte Wyatt come along slowly in their recovery from injuries, Campbell has been batting passes and turning heads. To this point in camp, Campbell has used his lengthy build to swat as many as four passes over the Packers’ last three practices while also showing up big in one-on-one matchups. He went 4-0 in individual pass rushing drills yesterday, according to Pete Dougherty , beating 2025 second round pick Anthony Belton twice, 2026 fifth rounder Jager Burton once, and 2026 undrafted free agent Josh Gesky once. That’s hardly a murderer’s row, but it’s nothing to sneeze at either; they’re not All-Pros, but Belton, Burton, and Gesky are all significant pieces of the Packers’ offensive line picture. But Campbell, to this point, has barely been in the picture at all, and that’s pretty much true of everywhere he’s been in his long football journey. Even in the picture I used for this article, Campbell (number 60) is an afterthought, but it’s literally the only image of him in the databases for either Getty Images or USA Today. He can’t even get top billing over the similarly unheralded Jaden Crumedy. So who is Campbell and how did he get here? A three-star recruit out of Florida’s Bartow High School, Campbell took a meandering path to the NFL. After a high school career that had him spending time at tight end and defensive end (highlighted by a 79-yard scoop and score fumble recovery), Campbell spent two years at Independence Community College in Kansas before landing at the University of Louisiana Monroe. In two seasons for the Warhawks, Campbell appeared in 17 games, recording 13 total tackles and the lone sack of his college career. After two years in Louisiana, Campbell transferred to Miami, putting him only about four hours from where he grew up. He’d play a small rotational role for the Hurricanes, appearing in just one game in 2023 and another eight in 2024. Though he’d total just 47 snaps as a senior, 10 came as a nose tackle, perhaps a nod to his bulked-up build; he’d played at 277 pounds at UL-Monroe, but was listed at an even 300 pounds at Miami. Campbell put up solid numbers in the 2025 pre-draft process, highlighted by a 9-foot, 3-inch broad jump and a decent 40-yard dash time to go with his prodigious frame. Still, pre-draft buzz was understandably hard to come by, and Campbell projected as an undrafted free agent. Dane Brugler rated him as the 115th best defensive lineman (out of 240) in the class in the 2025 edition of The Beast. Post-draft, Campbell landed with the Seahawks after minicamp tryouts with the Vikings and Eagles and spent the 2025 preseason there, playing 23 snaps across Seattle’s three exhibition games. He signed with the Seahawks’ practice squad on September 2, 2025, only to be released a day later in a series of transactions that will be of note to Packers fans. Former Packers defensive back Shemar Jean-Charles, current Packers running back Damien Martinez and one other player were released to make way for Campbell and two others on the Seattle practice squad, only for all six players to swap places again the very next day. Now, two of the six players involved are in Green Bay — the NFL world truly is small. Campbell finally arrived in Green Bay as a part of a flurry of late-season transactions leading up to the Packers’ playoff game against the Chicago Bears, joining the practice squad as o ne of 29 roster moves in a 13-day window . He didn’t appear in that playoff game — Isaiah Neyor was the only practice squad elevation — but the Packers thought enough of him to sign him to a reserve/future deal two days after their collapse in Chicago. Now, Campbell finds himself with a chance to make some noise in a defensive line group that can use all the help it can get. Defensive line has been a weakness in Green Bay for years, and injuries up front left them perilously thin at points last season. Nobody should count on Campbell to be a star, but if he can at least be a worthwhile depth piece, that’ll be a significant help to the Packers. He’ll have competition. Beyond Wyatt and Hargrave, 2026 third-round pick Chris McClellan is the only roster lock, but fourth-year Karl Brooks and second-year Warren Brinson should be considered good bets. That’s already five roster spots accounted for, leaving Campbell to compete with second-year Nazir Stackhouse and others for a job that may not even exist. But considering what he’s survived just to get to this point, it’s hard to bet against him. He’s come out of nowhere everywhere he’s been. What’s one more unexpected run to a roster spot?

title: The Packers need these rotational players to contribute in 2026
summary: The top of the Green Bay Packers’ depth chart is exciting, but it’s the backups and rotational players that could help them turn into a legitimate Super Bowl contender in 2026. Every team has star players, and while the Packers have some extremely bright ones in players like Micah Parsons, Tucker Kraft, and Jordan Love, […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers defensive end Barryn Sorrell (99) against the Washington Commanders on Thursday, September 11, 2025, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis. The Packers defeated the Commanders 27-18. Wm. Glasheen USA TODAY NETWORK-Wisconsin | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The top of the Green Bay Packers’ depth chart is exciting, but it’s the backups and rotational players that could help them turn into a legitimate Super Bowl contender in 2026. Every team has star players, and while the Packers have some extremely bright ones in players like Micah Parsons, Tucker Kraft, and Jordan Love, it takes all 11 players on the field at any time to find consistent success. So let’s look at a few of these depth pieces who need to have positive contributions during the year to help the Packers get their NFC North title back and become a dangerous contender. Skyy Moore Green Bay’s return units were extremely disappointing last season. Along with ranking just outside of the bottom ten in average kickoff return distance, the Packers were one of just three teams to have zero returns of 40-plus yards. As if that wasn’t bad enough, the Packers also ranked dead last on punt returns with an average return of just 5.6 yards. That’s not good enough. Skyy Moore comes into Green Bay as a proven return specialist. He averaged 11.64 yards per punt return last season while also returning a kickoff 98 yards for the San Francisco 49ers. On top of his return ability, Moore can still be an effective veteran receiver to back up the likes of Jayden Reed and Matthew Golden, as made evident by some of his one-on-one reps in practice on Tuesday. Skyy Moore in 1-on-1s today: pic.twitter.com/tasmj9iyxR — Kelly Hallinan (@kellyhals) August 4, 2026 He’s not going to be WR1 in Green Bay, but Moore’s special teams contributions alone should make him a valuable part of this roster. MarShawn Lloyd Is this finally going to be the year where we see a fully healthy MarShawn Lloyd? The former third-round pick out of USC has been plagued by injuries during his first two NFL seasons, appearing in just one game where he ran the ball six times for 15 yards. Along with nagging hamstring injuries and an ankle issue that landed him on injured reserve as a rookie, the running back also underwent an emergency appendectomy just as he was activated off of IR that same season. Lloyd has showed up to Packers training camp looking healthy, and reminded fans of the burst and speed that he brought with him from college that had the Packers taking him on Day 2 of the 2024 NFL Draft. #Packers RB MarShawn Lloyd getting in some work on the 5th training camp practice. pic.twitter.com/8AmzA1pQDg — Kyle Malzhan (@KyleMalzhan) August 3, 2026 That’s an ideal play style for a change-of-pace RB, and as long as he can stay on the field, the Packers can utilize Lloyd’s speed in a variety of ways. Barryn Sorrell Micah Parsons isn’t expected to be back for the Packers until at least Week 6, throwing a wrench in Green Bay’s pass-rush plans to start the year. That means that the rest of the Packers’ EDGEs need to step up, whether it’s Lukas Van Ness playing for an extension, Dani Dennis-Sutton trying to prove himself as a rookie, or Barryn Sorrell hoping to take a step forward after a quiet rookie year. Sorrell was a fourth-round pick out of Texas last year, appearing in 14 games and playing 206 defensive snaps. The production was modest on those reps, generating just seven pressures, seven defensive stops, and 1.5 sacks on the year. That doesn’t mean all hope is lost for the second-year EDGE. At 6-foot-4 and 260 pounds, Sorrell has ideal size out on the edge as a three-down player, and his flashes were awfully exciting last year. Barryn Sorrell is a #dawg pic.twitter.com/tTfZzzOUWe — Eli Berkovits (@BookOfEli_NFL) January 5, 2026 It needs to be a group effort from Green Bay’s EDGE room with Parsons on the PUP and Rashan Gary now in Dallas, but keep an eye on Sorrell as a potential breakout candidate early in the year.

title: Green Bay Packers news: Defense making its mark in training camp
summary: The Packers’ defense seems to be making a move here in the second week of training camp. It’s tough to put too much significance on headlines alone, but the panopticon of Packers’ media seems to have really turned its attention to the defense. It’s not enough to say whether or not the defense is actually […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon talks with head coach Matt LaFleur during practice on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. Tork Mason/USA TODAY NETWORK-Wisconsin | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Packers’ defense seems to be making a move here in the second week of training camp. It’s tough to put too much significance on headlines alone, but the panopticon of Packers’ media seems to have really turned its attention to the defense. It’s not enough to say whether or not the defense is actually good or bad or anything like that, but it feels noteworthy that a unit still without its best player is garnering this much attention in camp. I’m preaching to the choir when I say this, but the defense absolutely has to be good this year. The Packers have invested too many resources and too much time for anything short of a high quality unit, and too much depends on it for it to slack at all. This isn’t a team that’s going to have to be carried by the defense, but the more load the defense can carry, the more the offense can experiment and try different things as it sorts out its own identity. Of course, there is the lingering possibility that the defense is looking good because the offense is falling on its face in camp. There are certainly a few questions yet unresolved on that side of the ball, but let’s take the positive angle. The Packers’ defense is earning its attention through genuinely solid play, and it augurs well for the season ahead. Fingers crossed! full_text: There is probably not another sport where draft position matters more than in the NFL. In particular, number one overall picks specifically and those taken within the first handful of selections are graded very harshly. There aren’t that many Hall of Famers. There shouldn’t be. Still, first overall sections are expected to be Pro Bowl level players and should be in contention for the Hall of Fame. At least that is the expectation. If the Hall of Fame or the Pro Bowl is the bar then J.D. Clowney probably fails the test for a first overall pick. He officially has been to three Pro Bowls. That feels very light when you compare that with Aaron Donald who was also selected in the first round. However, he is going into his 13th season and he has been highly productive overall even if he hasn’t amassed the season to season high sack totals that were expected when he first came out of Clemson. Tackles TFL Sacks FF 2014 7 3 0.0 0 2015 40 8 4.5 1 2016 52 16 6.0 1 2017 59 21 9.5 2 2018 47 16 9.0 1 2019 31 7 3.0 4 2020 19 4 0.0 1 2021 37 11 9.0 2 2022 28 4 2.0 1 2023 43 9 9.5 2 2024 46 9 5.5 0 2025 41 12 8.5 1 Career 450 120 66.5 16 So, obviously these numbers are a mixed bag. On the one hand, it is impressive to put together a 13 year career (counting this season). Two of those seasons are a virtual wash due to injuries, so he has had a solid ten year career. Most players can’t approach that and most players from his draft are no longer in the league building their resume. The football Hall of Fame is not my personal wheelhouse like the baseball Hall of Fame, but if we look at the defensive ends and edge rushers in Canton then we will see that 100 sacks is usually the minimal litmus test to enter the door. In fact, if we look at the recent additions at the position over the last five seasons we can see what their career numbers are. Tackles TFL Sacks FF Jared Allen 648 171 136.0 31 Julius Peppers 719 175 159.5 51 Dwight Freeney 350 128 125.5 47 It’s at this point where I have to acknowledge two things. First, I absolutely love numbers. I think every reader of this feature realizes that. It eliminates a lot of the noise. When we look at these Hall of Famers we can see the clear separation between them and players like Clowney. We will also see guys like J.J. Watt fit comfortably in that group. Will Anderson certainly seems like he is on that path and Danielle Hunter is probably on that road as well. Tackles TFL Sacks FF J.J. Watt 586 195 114.5 27 Danielle Hunter 562 140 114.5 15 Will Anderson 136 46 30.0 4 Obviously, Anderson will take some projection since he has only finished three seasons. However, if we assume he continues on the pace he is on then the Texans have two Hall of Fame level defensive ends at or near the prime of their career. Watt obviously is now the number one CBS commentator, but his numbers serve as an area of reference. We say all this to say that Clowney is certainly a starting quality defensive end and has been one for a decade. The fact that he is the first end off the bench is a huge plus for the Texans in terms of depth. He probably won’t get the snaps he got in Dallas last season, but he certainly has been a productive player even if he isn’t a dominant one historically. He feels like a Mario Williams level of player in terms of being a very good performer that wasn’t consistently among the league’s best. Still, when you are a championship team, you need guys like Clowney. You need depth pieces that can come off the bench and perform to win a key game or two. It doesn’t work in this fay and age to have 11 good football players on each side and expect them to make it through the season healthy. Imagine a trade deadline in MLB and Nick Caserio got more done last week than anything happening over on Crawford street.

title: Houston Texans Stock Up, Stock Down after the first week of Training Camp
summary: The Texans have completed one week of Training Camp and it’s been a learning experience to say the least. Between the rookies showcasing their skills, the injuries, and the veteran additions this first week has been as exciting as tumultuous. The offense still needs to gel, but the defense looks as formidable as ever. Let’s […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 01: British Brooks #44, Woody Marks #4 and Jawhar Jordan #26 of the Houston Texans cross the field during Houston Texans training camp at Houston Methodist Training Center on August 01, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Texans have completed one week of Training Camp and it’s been a learning experience to say the least. Between the rookies showcasing their skills, the injuries, and the veteran additions this first week has been as exciting as tumultuous. The offense still needs to gel, but the defense looks as formidable as ever. Let’s see who’s rising and falling throughout the first week of Texans Training Camp. Stock Down: Texans PR Department As much as I prefer to start on an upward trajectory, this has to be addressed. The Texans constrained their media affiliates on what they can tweet and communicate regarding depth charts, player groupings, and roster configuration. Do they not realize there are eight practices open to the public and preseason games? Fans will find out sooner or later what they’re hiding. My hunch, first-rounder Keylan Rutledge doesn’t look good and is not participating with the first or second string. The Texans PR staff has told media they are to NOT report offensive line combinations during practice. So, if you want to know who’s starting on the offensive line then you need to come to practice. There will be A LOT of shuffling early on in camp. Also, Nick Caserio says… — Will Kunkel (@WillKunkelV) July 29, 2026 This is more illogical than embarrassing… and it’s fairly embarrassing. There are eight practices open to the public, who have no media affiliation nor restriction on posting on social media. Word is going to get out one way or another as to what’s happening at camp. If anything, trying to conceal it will only make fans search harder. Stock Up: Justin Watson, WR Watson in very short time and with even less production wedged himself onto this roster as an integral part of the system. His blocking and route running are highly valued assets by Offensive Coordinator Nick Caley. Plus, the injury to Jaylin Noel opened up more reps for the veteran. Depending on Noel’s timeline, Watson has the inside track to not only make the roster but start as the WR3. Stock Down: Special Teams Jaylin Noel, Jake Hansen, and M.J. Stewart all are hurt and likely out for quite a while. They were slated to be significant contributors on special teams this season and will miss time due to various injuries. Noel is Houston’s kick and punt returner, Hansen is a tackling menace, and Stewart is phenomenal on kickoff. Noel and Stewart should be back later this season, but this phrase has been negatively impacted and we aren’t three days into practice. Stock Up: Marte Mapu and Wade Woodaz. Thanks to injury attrition, MM and WW have gone from the fringes of the roster to the backup linebackers on defense. The foot injury to Jake Hansen and quad injury to E.J. Speed immediately zapped the depth of this group. Now both Mapu and Woodaz must step up to assume the role and reps of the two injured linebackers. Stock Down: Jake Hummel The special teams linebacker was in line to earn a roster spot due to all of the injuries and youth at the position. Unfortunately, he has been nowhere to be seen since the start of training camp. Not at practice, not at the facility, nothing. In the Rosterology 2.0, Hummel was a part of the “Last Four In” to make the team. Being a no-show through the first week won’t bode well for his stock. Stock Up: Defensive depth Texans signed DL Mario Edwards, LB Sione Takitaki, and DE Jadeveon Clowney this weekend in a trio of moves to bolster the front seven. Takitaki is the third former New England Patriots LB who found their way onto Houston’s roster. These moves add more talent to the already stacked defense and integrates veterans into the room. Couldn’t be more intrigued by what Clowney brings to the defense.

title: Seth McGowan is making his case in the Colts’ backfield
summary: Seth McGowan arrived in Indianapolis as a seventh-round pick, which usually means expectations are low and the path to a role is narrow from the beginning. Late-round running backs do not get much handed to them, especially when the starter is Jonathan Taylor and the offense already knows where its identity begins. McGowan was never […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 3: Indianapolis Colts running back Seth McGowan (20) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts training camp practice on August 3, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Seth McGowan arrived in Indianapolis as a seventh-round pick, which usually means expectations are low and the path to a role is narrow from the beginning. Late-round running backs do not get much handed to them, especially when the starter is Jonathan Taylor and the offense already knows where its identity begins. McGowan was never going to walk into training camp with a job waiting for him, but running back is also one of the few positions where a late-round player can climb quickly if the style, physicality and gamestyle translate. The Colts do not have a settled backup behind Taylor, and McGowan has already started building a case that he deserves to be part of that conversation. He led Kentucky with 725 rushing yards and 12 touchdowns last season, and the early camp buzz has centered on the way he runs: decisive, physical and willing to finish through contact. Shane Steichen summed up the appeal pretty clearly, saying McGowan is “not scared of contact,” which is exactly the kind of trait coaches want to see from a rookie back trying to earn trust. McGowan’s profile is not hard to understand. He is a bigger back who can get downhill and run behind his pads, but he is not just a short-yardage grinder. There is enough burst to win outside when the lane is there, which matters because the Colts do not need a backup who only gives them predictable carries between the tackles. They need someone who can keep the offense functional when Taylor is off the field, whether that means hammering inside runs, pressing the edge or making enough happen on his own when the blocking is not perfect. Rookie RB, Seth McGowan with a nice outside run 💨 pic.twitter.com/ViaWIsC8uw — Logan Hancock (@ProFanLogan) August 4, 2026 That is where the battle with DJ Giddens becomes important. Giddens, a 2025 fifth-round pick, has a similar general profile and came into the league with a tad more draft investment behind him, but he did very little last season and has not done enough to lock down the RB2 job. If McGowan looks more decisive, more physical or more explosive through camp and the preseason, the fact that he was picked in the seventh round will not hold him back. Jonathan Taylor’s comments about McGowan are also telling. Taylor reportedly compared him to David Montgomery, which does not mean McGowan is about to become Montgomery or that the Colts have already found a future starter. It does, however, give a pretty clear idea of what stands out. Montgomery has built a strong NFL career by being tough, decisive and difficult to bring down cleanly. He is not the flashiest back in the league, but he runs with conviction, finishes plays and consistently gets more than what is blocked. If Taylor sees even some of that in McGowan, it explains why the rookie is already getting attention. The timing matters too. Taylor is still the engine of the Colts’ offense, but he is entering the final year of his contract and has dealt with injuries in past seasons. The team has also talked about finding ways to take some of the workload off him, which only works if another running back earns real trust. The backup job is not just a roster footnote this year. It could mean six to eight touches a game, more work if Taylor misses time, and a much larger role next season if the Colts and Taylor do not work out another deal. That does not mean McGowan should be treated like the obvious future at running back before he has played an NFL game. He still has to prove the parts of the position that decide whether young backs actually get on the field, especially pass protection, ball security, consistency and special teams value. Running hard is a great starting point, but coaches need to know a rookie will not get the quarterback hit, catch a pass if needed or put the ball on the ground. The Colts need a real backup behind Taylor, Giddens has not separated himself, and McGowan has the kind of physical style that can show up quickly once the pads come on. He does not need to become the future starter right now. He just needs to prove he is too useful to ignore, and on a roster without a clear No. 2 back, that may be enough to make him one of the more interesting young players in Colts camp.
