full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JUNE 09: Maxx Crosby #98 of the Las Vegas Raiders looks on during mandatory minicamp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on June 09, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Louis Grasse/Getty Images) | Getty Images Recently, ESPN polled NFL types to rank the top 10 pass-rushers in the NF going into the 2026 season. Las Vegas Raiders’ star pass-rusher Maxx Crosby ranked No. 4 on the list. We ran a FEED post, asking our community members if they think the ranking of Crosby was fair. The general consensus among our FEED resposnes was, yes, the ranking of Crosby was fair. Yes, the primary judging criteria for pass-rushers is sack totals. Crosby had 10 sacks in 15 games last season, which was tied for the 15th most in the league. But there is so much more to playing edge than sack totals. Crosby had a career-high 28 tackles for loss in 2025, which was the second highest total in the NFL. He also rarely comes off the field and he is a complete player. There are many dominance pass-rushers in the NFL and, I agree with many of the readers, that Crosby is an elite defensive end and he is worthy of his high ranking. The specifics of the injury were not released, but head coach Jeff Hafley left no doubt that it would be season-ending. […]
full_text: Aug 16, 2025; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; New York Jets defensive tackle Fatorma Mulbah (62) following the game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Rich Barnes-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Miami Dolphins added defensive lineman Fatorma Mulbah to the roster on Wednesday, according to his agent Brett Tessler . The move comes a day after rookie defensive tackle Rene Konga suffered a serious injury. The specifics of the injury were not released, but head coach Jeff Hafley left no doubt that it would be season-ending. Hafley, after answering questions about injury status of some of the other players on the roster, added, “[Konga]’s the one [injury] that will be long term. He’ll be out for the season…But Konga will be done for the year, and that’s unfortunate because he’s a young guy who was working really hard and he’ll have to view this as a redshirt year.” Konga joined the Dolphins as an undrafted free agent this year. He started his college career at Rutgers before transferring to Louisville for the last two seasons. During the 2025 season, he recorded 29 tackles, 1.5 sacks, and six passes defensed in 12 games for Louisville; he was named Second-Team All-ACC after the season. The Dolphins have a lot of depth at defensive tackle, but Konga could have been fighting for a developmental spot on the roster or practice squad. Mulbah originally entered the league last year as an undrafted free agent out of West Virginia, signing with the New York Jets. He was cut by the team, but then returned to their practice squad in October before being released again in January. He spent the start of his college career at Penn State.

title: Dolphins shake up leadership group with new CEO named
summary: The Miami Dolphins on Tuesday shook up the top levels of the franchise in a move that probably should not have come as a surprise. After 13 years as the Dolphins’ President and Chief Executive Officer, Tom Garfinkel stepped down, paving the way for owner Stephen Ross to name Daniel Sillman to the top spot […]
full_text: Miami Dolphins owner Stephen M. Ross and Dolphins Vice Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer Tom Garfinkel talk before the start of an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday, Sept. 8, 2019 at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, Fla. (David Santiago/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) | TNS via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins on Tuesday shook up the top levels of the franchise in a move that probably should not have come as a surprise. After 13 years as the Dolphins’ President and Chief Executive Officer, Tom Garfinkel stepped down, paving the way for owner Stephen Ross to name Daniel Sillman to the top spot of football operations. Sillman, who led the team’s search for new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan and new head coach Jeff Hafley this offseason, has been named in the succession plan for the Dolphins should anything happen to Ross. Sillman was named the CEO of Ross Sports & Entertainment, a newly formed entity that brings the Dolphins, Hard Rock Stadium, the Miami Grand Prix, the Miami Open tennis tournament and the Precision Drive Club under one umbrella for Ross. Several members of Ross’s leadership team will now report to Sillman, which for the Dolphins including Sullivan, Hafley, and Executive Vice President of Football Operations Brandon Shore. While Garfinkel is stepping away from his day-to-day role with the Dolphins, he will remain as Vice Chairman for the Dolphins and Hard Rock Stadium. He will also remain as the managing partner for the Miami Grand Prix. Garfinkel’s work since becoming the President and CEO of the Dolphins was highlighted in the press release from the team. It read, “Since joining the Dolphins in 2013, Garfinkel spearheaded the business turnaround of the organization, including increasing annual revenues by more than 400 percent and securing more than $3 billion in future contractually obligated sponsorship income. Garfinkel led the vision and execution of the privately funded $550 million transformation of Hard Rock Stadium, oversaw the development of the $135 million Baptist Health Training Complex, and helped grow the Dolphins Cancer Challenge into the NFL’s largest charitable fundraiser, generating more than $100 million for cancer research. ” Garfinkel was also responsible for creation of the Miami Grand Prix for Formula 1 racing around Hard Rock Stadium and for bringing the Miami Open tennis tournament to Hard Rock Stadium. His efforts also resulted in the Dolphins’ home stadium hosting a Super Bowl, two College Football National Championship games, and seven matches during the 2026 World Cup including the third place game. “I love the Dolphins and the people here, but after 13 years it was just the right time for me to make this decision,” said Garfinkel via the press release. “The business has never been in a better place and the team of people we have here is second to none in sports. I want to thank the South Florida community and Dolphins fans for all of their support over the years and especially Steve Ross for the opportunity to be a part of this great organization. He is a visionary leader and a team owner who always strives to be best-in-class, and he provides his people all the trust and resources needed to be successful. I have every confidence in where this organization is headed on and off the field under Danny’s leadership, and I’m excited about the new challenges that will come moving forward.”

title: Vikings Training Camp Notes: 8/5 Edition
summary: The Minnesota Vikings had the most physical practice of training camp today, in full pads, and this one seemed to take on more importance than others as kind of the final test of the first week of training camp. Tomorrow is an off-day- no practice- but I wouldn’t be surprised if the coaching staff was […]
full_text: The Minnesota Vikings had the most physical practice of training camp today, in full pads, and this one seemed to take on more importance than others as kind of the final test of the first week of training camp. Tomorrow is an off-day- no practice- but I wouldn’t be surprised if the coaching staff was hard at work with evaluations and updated plans for the next part of training camp. So, let’s get into it. Quarterback Competition If you look at the readout of attempts and completions (below, compiled by Judd Zulgad) for Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy, you’d probably come to the conclusion that it was a pretty even day in the quarterback competition. It wasn’t. Murray: 14/21, including 11/15 in 11 on 11 and 3/6 in 7 on 7. McCarthy: 13/20, including 10/14 in 11 on 11 and 3/6 in 7 on 7. In fact, after today’s practice, I would not be surprised if Kevin O’Connell declares Kyler Murray the starting quarterback sometime in the next few days, perhaps even tomorrow. We’ll see. Kyler Murray The reason the quarterback competition wasn’t close today, despite the completion percentage stats indicating so, is first of all Kyler Murray threw for about a hundred more yards than J.J. McCarthy in 11-on-11 team drills, which are what really counts. Murray had two bombs- one to Tai Felton who was wide open on a post route that went for a long (50 yard-ish) touchdown, and another one later to Justin Jefferson that was really kind of a jump ball that Jefferson came down with over Isaiah Rodgers and Theo Jackson. Jefferson ran it in for a touchdown. . @JJettas2 ✈️✈️ pic.twitter.com/kOoqRGafil — Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) August 6, 2026 Looking at this video, it looked like Rodgers might have been a bit more cautious to avoid a collision/injury than he might have been in a real game, but still a nice play by Jefferson to come down with it. Kyler Murray to Tai Felton for the DEEP touchdown 👀 (Via Vikings mobile app) pic.twitter.com/iYFMG9f1vJ — VikingzFanPage (@vikingzfanpage) August 6, 2026 This last throw by Murray- hitting a receiver deep and in-stride- we haven’t seen since 2024 Sam Darnold. It looked like Isaiah Rodgers again in coverage but whether he was supposed to have help over the top is a question. If so, it looked like Josh Metellus, who came running late, missed the assignment. Murray’s other passes were mostly short, but a couple intermediate ones too including a TD pass to Jauan Jennings. His incompletions were on a middle screen that got blown up, an intermediate pass to Hockenson that was a bit low but Hockenson dropped it, a PBU by Charles Demmings on an intermediate pass targeting Jefferson, and a throw-away after a scramble in the red zone with nobody open. Murray again looked calm in the pocket- he actually held the ball a bit longer today than in other practices looking for the deep ball- and was able to move the offense well. No miscommunications or bad snaps or other mishaps today. He also scrambled and ran a few times after not finding an open receiver in team drills- once left, once right, and once up the middle. I didn’t see a would-be sack of Murray today either. J.J. McCarthy McCarthy’s completions in 11-on-11 team drills were mostly of the short variety, with a few intermediate passes mixed in. He also had two or three would-be sacks where the rusher broke it off because hitting quarterbacks is not allowed. But going back to my training camp notes on Monday , this was another McCarthy performance that looked very similar to his training camp performances last year. On most pass attempts, it simply looks like a struggle for him processing. There are some quick hitters when he does fine, but on most longer route concepts he holds the ball too long, waiting for a receiver to come open until he’s under pressure and opts for a checkdown. I don’t think he’s even attempted an over-the-top bomb since the start of training camp in 11-on-11 team drills. Last year in training camp there were usually one or two attempts each practice. Toward the end of 11-on-11 drills Kevin O’Connell talked to him a few times in-between plays. Judging by what happened on the previous play, it looked like O’Connell was trying to get him to speed up his processing. At one point he raised his hand to his head with his finger pointed toward his head moving in a circular motion indicating speed it up. There was even a completion over the middle to Jennings late in the down where O’Connell talked to him after the play seemingly to get him to speed things up. So, for the most part, 2026 training camp McCarthy is the same as 2025 training camp McCarthy, except no deep balls. His completion percentage may look fine, but it’s mostly screens and checkdowns. And the reason it’s mostly screens and checkdowns is because he’s too slow processing and isn’t able to throw with anticipation. Accuracy can be an issue on occasion- mostly on the longer throws he attempts, but that hasn’t been as big an issue in team drills this year primarily because he’s not throwing down the field much. There were no layered throws again today. What we are seeing is McCarthy having reached a plateau that isn’t high enough to be a quality starter. And until the light comes on and he’s able to process faster, he’s likely to remain at this level. So, Murray continues to separate himself and the first-team reps have been following that separation over the last 3-4 practices. I don’t know how much more Kevin O’Connell needs to see before he names Murray the starter, but I wouldn’t be surprised if he does so soon. That would allow Murray to get all the first-team reps going forward and help him continue to learn the offense and build rapport with the receivers he’ll be throwing to in the regular season. For McCarthy, the question becomes whether he or Carson Wentz would be the best backup. Battle in the Trenches Offensive and defensive linemen faced off today in full contact drills that were fun to watch- almost as fun as the special teams gunner drills- which I’ll get into later. The trench battles began with one-on-one pass rush/block drills. The Vikings website broke it down like this: Christian Darrisaw and Dallas Turner set the tone and traded blows out of the gate. On their initial rep, Darrisaw locked up a bull rush by the third-year OLB; Turner got him right back, winning with speed. Defensive lineman Levi Drake Rodriguez, who turned 26 Tuesday, took home the make-believe Best Move Award with a silky spin move past center Blake Brandel that landed him smack dab in the lap of an assistant coach acting as QB. Second-year DL Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins and guard Will Fries went back and forth, just like CD and DT, with the former executing a nice push-pull rush, and then the latter resetting his feet to win take No. 2. The strongest two-rep sequence belonged to 2025 UDFA Joe Huber, who shut down back-to-back rushes by 2026 first-round pick Caleb Banks. Huber sat down in his seat and cranked his feet on both occasions. Toward the end of the drill, Jalen Redmond and Turner stunted left down the line to squeeze past guard Donovan Jackson and Darrisaw and reach the QB in a timely manner. Earlier, Jackson outlasted Redmond twice. title: Wonder About the Over/Under
summary: The crew at the Daily Norseman is doing its usual stellar job covering the opening days of training camp, including an increasingly intriguing quarterback competition. The same goes for the news that the Vikings brought in safety Jamal Adams and extended offensive tackle Brian O’Neill. We’re so back. This allows me to vent a little. […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 01: Head coach Kevin O'Connell of the Minnesota Vikings looks on during Training Camp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on August 01, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The crew at the Daily Norseman is doing its usual stellar job covering the opening days of training camp, including an increasingly intriguing quarterback competition . The same goes for the news that the Vikings brought in safety Jamal Adams and extended offensive tackle Brian O’Neill. We’re so back. This allows me to vent a little. The topic? The Vikings’ head-scratching over/under of 8.5 wins for the upcoming season. I’ve noted several times over the past year or so how astute the oddsmakers are. They tend to know what they’re doing, whether it’s good or bad for the team(s) you root for. This time, I’m truly at a loss. Take last year, when the over/under was 8.5 wins early in the offseason and 9.5 wins in some places just before Week 1. Did I agree with it? Nope. Chugging a gallon or 12 of purple Kool-Aid (as always) was a contributing factor. Did I understand it? Absolutely. Rolling with a first-time, unproven starter at quarterback alone was enough to justify a healthy drop from 14 wins the year prior. Known unknowns were there. And guess what? The oddsmakers were right on, and yours truly was wrong. I had them at 12, while it took a Week 18 home win over a Green Bay Packers team already locked in the 7th seed for the over to hit at 9-8… or not, if you didn’t get in early. TOO MUCH NEEDS TO HAPPEN FOR THE UNDER Fast-forward to now, and the Vikings are again staring at an 8.5 over/under for the 2026 season. That is dead last in the NFC North, behind the Lions at 10.5, the Packers at 9.5, and the Bears at 9.5. Gross. Unlike last year and most years before it, I can’t get my head around the logic this time. The Vikings entered the 2025 season with a strength of schedule ranked 4th- to 7th-hardest, depending on the metrics used (e.g., opponents’ prior-year winning percentage vs. projected over/under). This year, it’s ranked 11th to 17th. As I noted previously, the overall quarterback play in 2025 was the worst since at least 2013, probably 2007. And those offenses were run-first, Adrian Peterson-led units. The numbers tell the story. Last year, per Statmuse, the McCarthy- (mostly injured) Wentz- Brosmer trifecta managed only 3,200 gross passing yards, about 1,200 fewer than in 2024. Gross is the keyword here. This ranked 30th in passing yards per game. Meanwhile, the Vikings ranked 28th in EPA per play. We went 9-8 and missed the playoffs by ½ game. For the Vikings to not match that mark and therefore not hit the over for 2026, most, if not all, of the following will need to occur: QUARTERBACK/OFFENSIVE PERFORMANCE (REGARDLESS OF STARTER) Kyler Murray, a former #1 overall pick with over 20,000 career passing yards, a 67% completion percentage, and a 2:1 TD-INT ratio, will need to be so bad in this offense that he gets benched. This would defy historical precedent, given what KOC has done with veterans such as Sam Darnold and Nick Mullens. J.J. McCarthy, who was 6-4 as a starter despite the struggles, will have to make zero improvement during an offseason when he made it a priority to do just that. No additional comfort or growth in KOC’s offense in his third year. No progress in mechanics. No development. Zilch. Nada. Carson Wentz, if called upon for whatever reason, healthy and with a full offseason in the system, will somehow not be able to reach the level of “passable” when he had little trouble getting the ball to Justin Jefferson when he could actually move last season. The best WR trio in the NFL – and the Vikings’ best since Carter-Moss-Reed – will not only fail to live up to the hype but also embrace mediocrity. This says nothing of the depth advantage of having three receivers with experience in the #1 role (Addison in 2023, when Jefferson got hurt; Jauan Jennings on the 49ers in 2024). The offensive line will need to regress a year after its best player, Christian Darrisaw, was nowhere near 100% and is now, by all accounts, healthy. Donovan Jackson’s development will need to stall. Will Fries and Brian O’Neill would both need to have subpar seasons. Blake Brandel underperforming as the starting center – despite a full offseason of work – is a far more likely scenario, but nowhere near an insurmountable obstacle. The Vikings have been navigating less-than-stellar center play for years. DEFENSIVE PERFORMANCE Question marks along the defensive line are real. The Vikings could have kept either Jonathan Allen or Javon Hargrave, but the internal calculations clearly led them to pursue the current course. Both Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange will need to make limited contributions, while Jalen Redmond and the established depth will need to perform worse than expected for it to reach crisis level. It could happen, but a slight regression is more likely. Allen and Hargrave didn’t exactly have All-Pro seasons, either. Dallas Turner will need to be a far worse and more inconsistent replacement for Jonathan Greenard than expected. I’ve been on record as not favoring the decision to trade Greenard away (especially given the return), and I assume regression. Still, I don’t expect the pass rush to collapse in a way that would dramatically impact overall defensive performance. Brian Flores is adept at finding unique and unpredictable ways to pressure the quarterback. Which leads me to… Brian Flores would need to forget how to coach defense. He came here and promptly turned an atrocious defense that ranked 28th in points and 31st in yards into one that ranked 13th and 16th, respectively. The following two seasons brought Top 10 finishes in points (5th and 7th) and defensive DVOA (2nd and 6th). Adding a schematically versatile player like Jamal Adams not only addresses a potential Harrison Smith retirement but also an underwhelming Dallas Turner showing (Adams has 22.5 career sacks). Of course, as we’re the Vikings, there is always precedent for awful things. We watched Mike Zimmer lose his fastball in rapid, dramatic, 2015 Peyton Manning-esque fashion. I could write another 1,000 words on why I don’t think this will happen with Flores, but let’s say it would be… a stretch. MAKE IT MAKE SENSE I can’t understand it. Far, far, far more would have to go wrong for the Vikings not to hit the over on 8.5 wins. Can it happen? Definitely. This franchise has watched its stadium roof collapse, missed its first-round draft pick, inadvertently created the 1990s Dallas Cowboys dynasty, and remains the pacesetter for improbable, gut-wrenching, heartbreaking playoff losses. Going 8-9 or worse and missing the playoffs would be nothing for us. That said, this team is too well-coached and has too much talent. The Vikings have effectively taken out an insurance policy against the only thing that could prevent 9 wins by how they’ve assembled the quarterback room. Or maybe I’m just delusional.

title: Drake Maye weighs in on Kayshon Boutte’s future with Patriots
summary: New England Patriots wide receiver Kayshon Boutte has been at the center of trade speculation throughout the offseason. The 24-year-old enters the final year of his rookie contract and requested a trade during the spring after the Patriots acquired A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason. For now, though, Boutte remains in New England. Throughout […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JANUARY 18: Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots celebrates with Kayshon Boutte #9 after his touchdown catch against the Houston Texans during an NFL divisional playoff game at Gillette Stadium on January 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts.(Photo By Winslow Townson/Getty Images) | Getty Images New England Patriots wide receiver Kayshon Boutte has been at the center of trade speculation throughout the offseason. The 24-year-old enters the final year of his rookie contract and requested a trade during the spring after the Patriots acquired A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason. For now, though, Boutte remains in New England. Throughout training camp, the wide receiver has continued to flash his big-play ability while rotating with the first- and second-team offense as the Patriots wide receiver depth chart remains seven deep. That could still result in Boutte being elsewhere by Week 1. Following Wednesday’s walkthrough, quarterback Drake Maye was asked about Boutte’s future with the team. “I think just the way Kayshon is approaching it, man. He’s here now,” Maye said. “He’s where his feet are at, and I’m having fun throwing it to him out there in practice. He’s doing a great job, and he makes plays when the football’s in the air. And I think he can speak for that, and that speaks for itself. So, I’ve had a lot of great times with Kayshon, and I’m looking forward to us getting better each and every day.” After Boutte posted back-to-back 500-yard season, the Patriots added Brown and Doubs to the roster this season to join him, Mack Hollins, DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams, and Efton Chism III. Speaking earlier this week on SiriusXM NFL Radio, Maye broke down his top seven wide receivers and mentioned Boutte last. “Probably the last one is Boutte,” Maye said. “He’s a comforting receiver to throw to. You get to know him – same thing as Pop, this is my third year with Boutte and I was throwing to him on scout team when I was a rookie. Now we’re making plays; I threw my first touchdown to him. He’s just one of those guys that is quiet, does everything the right way, cares about his teammates, and he just puts his head down and works. There’s a lot of talk about whatever you want to say with Boutte, but he just continues to make plays. He’s going to be in the right spot and make a play on the football.” Maye’s comments echo what Boutte has shown throughout training camp. But the business side of the NFL could still result in him playing elsewhere before the regular season — something Boutte remains open to as he looks to secure the first significant payday of his career.

title: 7 performances of note from the Patriots’ 10th training camp practice
summary: The New England Patriots toned down the tempo on Wednesday. Coming off five practices in full pads, they went to bucket hats and T-shirts instead — an attire that reflected the intensity: the Patriots’ 10th session of training camp was a walkthrough. To recap the action, please check out our practice recap. In the meantime, […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots cornerback Channing Canada (29) walks to practice for training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots toned down the tempo on Wednesday. Coming off five practices in full pads, they went to bucket hats and T-shirts instead — an attire that reflected the intensity: the Patriots’ 10th session of training camp was a walkthrough. To recap the action, please check out our practice recap . In the meantime, here is who caught our eyes for better or worse. Standout of the day N/A: Unlike the last few days, the focus on Wednesday was not on competition. We did get a look at the depth chart and where the camp competitions currently stand, but the nature of the session prevents us from crowning a standout of the day. Other performances of note RB Terrell Jennings: After returning from the non-football injury list earlier this week, Jennings has been used quite prominently. On Wednesday, he was with the starting offense alongside Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson — an honor not reserved for any of the other backup RBs — and also lined up with the top kickoff return unit and the top punt block squad. The third-year man appears to be carving out an advantage in the race for the third running back spot. WR Efton Chism III: With Romeo Doubs missing the session, the Patriots had an opening in their starting lineup. It went to sophomore Efton Chism, whose ability to line up all over the formation has made him a valuable presence in the wide receiver room. Chism was with the starting wide receiver group during the first period of 11-on-11s and often was on the field in Doubs’ place alongside A.J. Brown and DeMario Douglas. It will be seen how his role evolved once Doubs is back, but his usage on Wednesday was definitively noteworthy. WR Kyle Williams: Even with Romeo Doubs absent, Kyle Williams was not among the group of wideouts repping with Drake Maye and the starters during the aforementioned 11-on-11s. He did join the top unit later, but did not line up against the starting defense. What he did do, however, was lining up as the first-unit kickoff returner alongside Terrell Jennings. The more you can do. CB Channing Canada and CB Karon Prunty: When the Patriots split into 11-on-11 work, the rookie pair was among the five cornerbacks to work with the defensive starters; Christian Gonzalez, Charles Woods and Marcus Jones were also part of the group. Both youngsters took the field behind Woods, the current CB4 and a top-level perimeter player with Carlton Davis still out, and are perhaps in the process elevating themselves beyond the other backups at the position. S Dell Pettus and S Mike Brown: The fight for the third safety spot saw Pettus and main competitor Mike Brown on different fields Wednesday. Whereas Pettus was with the first-teamers on defense, Brown was with the second unit. Both also served as the personal punt protectors, with Brown the top option at the position and Pettus — who filled that role during his 2024 rookie season — serving as the No. 2. The Patriots will hold their 11th practice of training camp on Thursday, and it will once again take place behind closed doors. Of course, Pats Pulpit will be on hand to report from the session.

title: Patriots training camp recap: Walkthrough provides look at depth chart
summary: After five straight fully padded practices the New England Patriots dialed it back on Wednesday with another walkthrough style practice. While the tempo was slowed, the session did provide an updated look at the depth chart as work was split between two fields. Here’s what went down throughout the session. Attendance Absent: WR Romeo Doubs […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2025; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Efton Chism III (86) warns up during minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect After five straight fully padded practices the New England Patriots dialed it back on Wednesday with another walkthrough style practice. While the tempo was slowed, the session did provide an updated look at the depth chart as work was split between two fields. Here’s what went down throughout the session. Attendance Absent: WR Romeo Doubs (new), CB Carlton Davis III, TE Jack Westover, OG Caedan Wallace, WR Cameron Dorner Returnee: FB Reggie Gilliam (rest), TE C.J. Dippre (PUP) PUP/NFI: ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler Wide receiver Romeo Doubs was a new absence during Wednesday’s walkthrough while the rest of the attendance list remained the same beyond fullback Reggie Gilliam (rest) returning. Gilliam shared his managed workload this summer was due to nagging injuries from recent years. Tight end C.J. Dippre was present at practice in uniform for the first time this summer indicating that he has been activated off the PUP list . Takeaways Chism and the WRs: With Romeo Doubs sidelined, Efton Chism III was the biggest beneficiary seeing plenty of snaps in the veteran’s place with the first-team offense — often sharing the field with A.J. Brown and DeMario Douglas. Chism’s ability to play/backup multiple wide receiver spots in the offense and him being counted on for his run blocking ability in packages with the first-team offense this camp has him on the path towards a roster spot. Drake Maye largely worked with A.J. Brown, Mack Hollins, Kayshon Boutte, Douglas, and Chism, while Kyle Williams originally started on the opposite field before working with Maye later on as the entire offense gathered together. RB rotation: Two days after being activated off the NFI list, Terrell Jennings joined Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson with Maye’s offense. Jennings is New England’s only depth running back with NFL experience and may have an early lead on the RB3 spot. Lan Larison, Jam Miller, and Myles Montgomery then repped on the opposite field. Rookie corners: As Carlton Davis remained absent, Charles Woods continued to operate as the top cornerback opposite of Christian Gonzalez. A pair of rookies in Karon Prunty and Channing Canada then worked in behind them with the first-team defense. Since the pads came on, Prunty has been around the ball often while Canada has also been competitive in coverage — although was on the wrong side of multiple completions in Tuesday’s session. Both seem to be trending upward as the team looks for depth behind their top corners. Special teams: Plenty of special teams work throughout the walkthrough. With the kicking game playing a big factor for those fighting for roster spots, the units included: Top punt block: Reggie Gilliam, Khalil Jacobs, Chad Muma, Elijah Ponder, Namdi Obiazor, Terrell Jennings Personal protectors: Mike Brown (top), Dell Pettus Kick returners: Kyle Williams and Terrell Jennings, Efton Chism III and Lan Larison, Kobe Prentice, Myles Montgomery, Channing Canada, DeMario Douglas Other notes: Offensive tackle Will Campbell wore a Rob Gronkowski-like arm brace on his left arm. The top two offensive lines remained the same: Campbell-Vera-Tucker-Wilson-Onwenu-Moses and Bryant-Rupcich-Brown-Hudson-Lomu. Gabe Jacas largely worked with the second-team defense and punt block unit. Dell Pettus mixed in behind Craig Woodson and Kevin Byard, perhaps signaling he has elevated to the No. 3 safety. They ended practice repping Hail Mary situations. The Patriots will be back on the practice fields on Thursday where they will be back in shells, which is set to begin at 10:15 a.m. ET.

Schedule Unlike Tuesday’s practice, Wednesday’s walkthrough will be closed to the public. For more information, please visit our Pats Pulpit Training Camp Guide . Story of the day What is the depth chart looking like? Due to the walkthrough nature of practice, there will be little competition in Foxborough on Wednesday. That does not mean we won’t get a glimpse at those competitions, though: players do line up in order of their supposed position on the current depth chart, and somebody playing regularly with the starters or the third-stringers is indicative of their chances of making the roster. Injuries to monitor NFI: S Brenden Schooler PUP: TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III Practice absentees: FB Reggie Gilliam, WR Cameron Dorner (new), TE Jack Westover (new), OL Caedan Wallace, CB Carlton Davis III The Patriots added two more players to their absentees list on Tuesday, with wideout Cameron Dorner and tight end Jack Westover missing the session. Whether or not their non-participation is due to injury is not known at this point, but the team added another depth receiver — Tejhaun Palmer — as a waiver claim after practice. Players to watch WR Kyle Williams and WR Efton Chism III: Williams and Chism have repped as the sixth and seventh receivers on the roster fairly consistently over the first nine practices. Wednesday will therefore provide as a chance to see whether or not anything has changed, especially with Williams having spent Monday’s session as a spectator. LB K.J.Britt and LB Khalil Jacobs: With Chad Muma seemingly starting to separate himself in the race for the third linebacker spot, veteran free agent Britt and undrafted rookie Jacobs might be dueling it out for the fourth and possibly final job. The backup cornerbacks: The backups options at cornerback are mentioned here for a second straight day, and for good reason. The competition for a fifth and sixth spot on the depth chart seemingly remains wide open. Inconsistency is the main reason for that, with Karon Prunty, Kindle Vildor, Kobee Minor, Channing Canada and Marcellas Dial Jr. all having their ups and downs so far this summer. title: How DeMario Douglas willed himself into a Patriots starting role
summary: Despite coming off a productive two-year stretch to open his NFL career, DeMario Douglas failed to find similar success in his first season under head coach Mike Vrabel and offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels. Between 2023 and 2024, Douglas had started 14 total games and was on the field for almost 60% of the New England […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 28: New England Patriots wide receiver DeMario Douglas at training camp on July 28, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images Despite coming off a productive two-year stretch to open his NFL career, DeMario Douglas failed to find similar success in his first season under head coach Mike Vrabel and offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels. Between 2023 and 2024, Douglas had started 14 total games and was on the field for almost 60% of the New England Patriots’ offensive snaps when healthy. In 2025, he started exactly zero games and played a mere 27% of snaps. He furthermore registered career-lows in targets (55) and catches (39). What was the problem? For Douglas, the adaptation to a new system under McDaniels proved to be a challenge. Fast forward a year, and he finds himself in an entirely different position. “I feel way more comfortable. Last year, I was really just getting the feel of it. Not really much of going through it,” Douglas explained after the Patriots’ ninth training camp practice on Tuesday. “Josh and [Todd Downing], they’ve been doing a great job of sitting us down and letting us break down the option routes.” So far in his fourth training camp, Douglas has been a fixture among the Patriots’ starters. Predominately lining up in the slot, he has been a heavily-featured part of the passing game alongside fellow top-level wideouts A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. That did not happen by accident. In fact, Mike Vrabel believes it is a logical continuation of his 2025 season. “I think the most impressive thing was that he was ready, whether he got 12 snaps or he got 30 snaps,” he explained. “I think some of his best plays were his ability to not catch the football and go and finish. He made plenty of plays for us, but his attitude remained really good. I know that every receiver wants to get the ball more.” This spring and summer, Douglas has been getting the ball on a fairly regular basis. While Brown and Doubs continue to build their chemistry with quarterback Drake Maye, the former sixth-round draft pick is feeding off their first two seasons together. Now entering his third year with Maye, he says that a variety of reasons played into this development — from finding a routine that works for him, to maximizing his own 5-foot-8, 185-pound body, to turning into one of the veterans in the room. Add a player deeply invested in his craft and his team, and you get the 2025 version of DeMario Douglas. “The team means everything to me,” he said. “It’s my family away from my family. I have their back, and I know for sure they have my back. I’m only one call away. I make sure I get to know all of my teammates’ names, just in case. you never know what may happen; if we depart I’m only one call away. … “I don’t work hard for nothing. I try to relay it to the game. In the offseason when we work out, I make sure that I’m competing against myself and somebody else — somebody else that wants to get better than me. I feel like I just have to keep working and it shows on the field. ” The results thus far have been promising, but Douglas will need to keep building on them. He did, after all, spend last year’s training camp as the top slot receiver as well. We all know how that turned out. That said, is seems to be a clear difference between both his own and the team’s approach to his role this time around. “I think we will continue to try to find ways for Pop to help us and then look at where he can continue to improve,” said Vrabel. “But nobody cares more about the team than Pop Douglas. I think that shows by the way he plays.”

title: Gabe Jacas grateful to be practicing with Patriots at training camp
summary: New England Patriots second-round pick Gabe Jacas has seen his workload steadily increase since making his training camp debut on Saturday. Tuesday marked the rookie’s highest participation level yet after signing his rookie contract on July 26, being one of the final two rookies in the NFL to reach a deal Jacas saw a handful […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 3: New England Patriots linebacker Gabe Jacas at training camp on August 3, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images New England Patriots second-round pick Gabe Jacas has seen his workload steadily increase since making his training camp debut on Saturday. Tuesday marked the rookie’s highest participation level yet after signing his rookie contract on July 26 , being one of the final two rookies in the NFL to reach a deal Jacas saw a handful of reps with the second-team defense during team periods on Tuesday and was also out on the field for the unit’s end-of-practice two-minute drill, holding Tommy DeVito’s offense to a successful field goal attempt with 1:05 on the clock. “First and foremost, I just want to say how grateful I am to be here,” Jacas said after practice. “It was a long journey, but I’m just glad to be here, be part of this organization, be at practice and run around.” The Illinois product dealt with a pre-draft hamstring injury; however, ESPN’s Mike Reiss wrote in June that Jacas also underwent a cleanup knee procedure. Furthermore, the Patriots inserted a left knee injury waiver into his rookie deal, as later reported by Reiss . When frequently asked about his medical status and missing extensive time with the team this offseason, Jacas repeatedly said that situation is behind him, and his knee is “good.” “I mean, it doesn’t matter. All that stuff is behind me, and whatever happened in the past is just the past. Trying to look forward and focus on the future … I’m 100%. Whenever they tell me I’m good to go, I just go.” The 22-year-old later added that he doesn’t have any long-term concerns with his knee. “We’ve got to make up for lost time, I think, a little bit with Gabe,” head coach Mike Vrabel said Tuesday of what he’s seen from the rookie. “I’d say he’s working hard. I think he’s into it. He’s trying to learn. He’s focused. A lot of these things are new for him, and I think he has done a good job of controlling what he can control. “He’ll have a few more reps than he did yesterday and – these situations he has to just understand, and it’s good to see him get acclimated to the special teams stuff. I think we’re off to a good start, and hopefully he can continue to keep adding things and figure out where he can help us defensively and really, special teams.” Vrabel has spent extensive one-on-one time with Jacas working on punt team reps to make sure the rookie is caught up in that area. He explained it’s one of the toughest things for young players to learn. And in that process of Jacas getting acclimated to the team environment, it’s clear his relationships with his coaches are growing. “You can tell Vrabel’s a very hands-on coach,” he said. “I’m just appreciative that he can just take me to the side and teach me a couple techniques and [how to] be a better punt protector so I can be better for this team.” During Jacas’ first practice on Saturday, he accidentally bull-rushed through outside linebackers coach Mike Smith’s blocking pad. Smith fell to the ground as the rookie showed off the brute power that made him a standout player at Illinois with 27 career collegiate sacks. One practice later, on Monday, Smith got his revenge during a drill, wrapping Jacas up and tackling the rookie onto a landing pad as the two threw fake punches at one another. “That wasn’t my intention,” Jacas said about knocking Smith over. “But when you’re just getting off the ball and violent, stuff like that happens. That’s what happens when you’re coached by Mike Smith, who is a very good coach.” Before Jacas’ first session with the team, Vrabel revealed last week that outside linebacker would continuously text him late at night after signing his rookie contract, asking if he was practicing the next day. Jacas told the media that it came from his eagerness to practice and play football again. “I just want to let all the Patriots fans know that I’m all behind everybody, and you’re going to get the best player out of me each and every game,” Jacas said in his message to the fan base. “And just anything I can do to help the team win, then I’m going to do it. Whatever it takes.”

title: TreVeyon Henderson feeling game slow down in second NFL season
summary: TreVeyon Henderson does most things fast. The running back ran a 4.43-second 40-yard dash before the Patriots selected him in the second round of the 2025 NFL Draft. That speed helped him become the first Patriot to score four touchdowns of 50-plus yards as a rookie. Mentally, though, things seemed to be moving too fast […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 25: New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson at training camp on July 25, 2026. (Photo by John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images TreVeyon Henderson does most things fast. The running back ran a 4.43-second 40-yard dash before the Patriots selected him in the second round of the 2025 NFL Draft. That speed helped him become the first Patriot to score four touchdowns of 50-plus yards as a rookie. Mentally, though, things seemed to be moving too fast at times. Henderson went through challenging stretches as a rookie, culminating in him playing just 30 total snaps across the AFC Championship Game and Super Bowl. Now entering Year 2, everything is beginning to slow down. “Most definitely,” he said. “I think the biggest thing is, like I said, understanding the offense a lot more, understanding certain plays, and then of course just continuing to get accustomed to the speed. I think by now I’m definitely accustomed, just being able to get a lot of opportunities last year. And so going into this year, just being a lot more patient, knowing what I’m doing, knowing where I’m supposed to be.” After helping Ohio State win the national championship in January 2025, Henderson immediately shifted his focus to preparing for the NFL. He went on to appear in all 21 games as a rookie, leaving little time to take a step back. This past offseason finally gave him that opportunity, and allowed Henderson to recover physically and sharpen his mental side of his game. “I think understanding the offense,” Henderson said. “Understanding certain runs and pass schemes and things like that — it’s been helping me a lot. I’m just trying to continue to enhance my game however I can.” While Henderson showcased his home-run ability as a ball carrier, he was not able to make the same impact in the passing game last season. Much of that was due to issues in pass protection. Early in training camp, the Patriots defense has not been shy about dialing up pressure from all over the field, giving Henderson plenty of opportunities to continue developing in that area. “It helps us a lot,” Henderson shared. “Whatever they throw at us, just being able to step up in the pocket and pick it up and protect the quarterback, that’s a big thing. So I’m just continuing to try to get better at that as well, each and every practice. It’s been helpful. “Just continuing to get opportunities, and when I get opportunities take advantage of it. Even when I’m not in, taking mental reps. Seeing what the defense is doing, going through my steps, going through my reads.”

title: Jeremiah wright’s injury puts Saints’ interior line depth under the microscope
summary: New Orleans Saints rookie guard Jeremiah Wright suffered an apparent shoulder injury during Wednesday’s practice, causing him to make an early exit. While the severity of the injury has yet to be determined, Wright’s departure is noteworthy because of the role he was expected to play this season. Selected in the fourth round of the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - MARCH 01: Jeremiah Wright #OL56 of Auburn participates in a drill during the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine at Lucas Oil Stadium on March 1, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images New Orleans Saints rookie guard Jeremiah Wright suffered an apparent shoulder injury during Wednesday’s practice, causing him to make an early exit. While the severity of the injury has yet to be determined, Wright’s departure is noteworthy because of the role he was expected to play this season. Selected in the fourth round of the recent NFL Draft out of Auburn, the versatile interior lineman entered camp as one of the team’s most intriguing young depth pieces. His absence is magnified by the uncertainty surrounding starting right guard Cesar Ruiz. After showing flashes of being a dependable starter throughout his NFL career, Ruiz’s consistency has remained an issue. Injuries have also interrupted his development in recent seasons, making reliable depth behind him an important priority for New Orleans. That’s where Wright entered the picture. At Auburn, Wright developed a reputation as a physical, technically sound blocker capable of handling multiple responsibilities along the interior offensive line. Those traits made him an ideal developmental prospect and someone who could compete for playing time while serving as insurance if injuries struck the starting lineup. If Wright is forced to miss time, the Saints could lose valuable developmental reps for a rookie who was expected to push for a role throughout training camp and the preseason. Just as importantly, it would leave the team’s interior depth a bit thinner behind Ruiz at a position where durability has already been a concern. The Saints are undoubtedly hoping Wright’s shoulder injury proves to be nothing more than a minor setback. But until more is disclosed, his exit from practice serves as a reminder of how quickly depth can become a pressing issue along the offensive line.

title: Why Saints football matters
summary: Mondays during football season hit just a little differently. The excitement of looking forward to the upcoming game fills the week with anticipation and energy. It takes away the mental hurdles of planning what needs to be done around the house. It gives husbands a built-in excuse to put off the household chores their wives […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - MAY 08: A general overall exterior view of Caesars Superdome and the New Orleans skyline on May 08, 2024 in New Orleans, Louisiana. Caesars Superdome will host Super Bowl LIX on February 9, 2025. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Mondays during football season hit just a little differently. The excitement of looking forward to the upcoming game fills the week with anticipation and energy. It takes away the mental hurdles of planning what needs to be done around the house. It gives husbands a built-in excuse to put off the household chores their wives may need them to do or the places they may want them to go. Sons get excited to share those moments with their dads or brothers. Sisters look forward to their brothers staying out of the way on the weekends. Throughout the week, conversations are filled with either the game that just happened or the one that is coming up. In the South, especially in Louisiana, football—from park ball to college—takes over the entire week from August through December. Friday night lights set the stage as the appetizer for the weekend. Once the high school games wrap up, all eyes turn to Sunday. Football brings communities together. But it’s hard to find a community that is as deeply connected to its team as the Saints are with New Orleans. In New Orleans, your Monday after a Saints game is completely dependent on how successful the Saints were on Sunday. If they win, it could be storming, raining, and miserable outside, yet somehow it still feels like one of the best Mondays of the year. If they lose, it could be 75 degrees with no humidity and not a cloud in the sky, and you’d still find a way to get stuck behind every garbage truck, hit every red light, and drive through every school zone all day long. During those days, you’re surrounded by people who share the same emotions, whether it’s the joy of victory or the pain of defeat. Football brings us together. The experience of being a Saints season ticket holder is truly life changing. You don’t just find fellow fans—you develop an extended family. These are people you look forward to seeing nine weekends out of the year, and when they aren’t there, you’re reaching out because you’re genuinely concerned about their well-being. Even if you’re not a season ticket holder but have a regular place where you watch the games every Sunday, those same relationships begin to form. Before long, you’re sharing birthday pictures, making holiday plans, and spending time together outside of football season just to keep that community thriving during the offseason. Whether it’s the emotional highs of Steve Gleason blocking the punt, Garrett Hartley making the field goal, or Tracy Porter returning the interception for a touchdown—moments from games I know I don’t even have to explain—you remember exactly where you were and who you were with. The same is true for the painful moments. The Minneapolis Miracle. The Kyle Rudolph push-off. The NOLA No- Call. The pain of those moments felt like grieving the loss of a loved one, and it was those bonds with fellow fans that helped you get through it. For those who aren’t as invested, they simply don’t understand the emotional toll moments like that can have. Football is a game at its core, but it’s bigger than that. It’s part of the fabric of our culture, a lifeline in our society, and a thread of commonality that connects us all and gives us something to build upon. Football has changed lives, even for people who never played or coached the game but simply watched it. Entire businesses have been built because of football, and it has created opportunities for people who otherwise may never have had them—or even thought to pursue them. Football provides a foundation for a community to truly show its best. That will be on full display this Saturday as Saints fans around the world celebrate the first former player in franchise history to become a first-ballot Pro Football Hall of Fame inductee, Drew Brees. The season is finally upon us. The days won’t feel quite as long, the temperatures won’t be quite as hot, and the weekends will once again be filled with life.

title: NY Giants training camp, practice No. 7: Odell Beckham has his best day
summary: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — The New York Giants completed their third consecutive day of padded practices, the maximum allowed by the Collective Bargaining Agreement, on Wednesday. This was the best day of camp for the offense, and for wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. Winners Beckham — This was Beckham’s best day of camp. He […]
full_text: Odell Beckham | Getty Images WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — The New York Giants completed their third consecutive day of padded practices, the maximum allowed by the Collective Bargaining Agreement, on Wednesday. This was the best day of camp for the offense, and for wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr . Winners Beckham — This was Beckham’s best day of camp. He caught passes from Jaxson Dart, Jameis Winston, and Brandon Allen, and showed some burst turning a couple of those receptions upfield. Yes, Beckham received some first-team reps on Wednesday, the second straight day that has happened. I refuse to fuss about that, though. Jalin Hyatt and Xavier Gipson also got first-team reps. Jaxson Dart — After he fired a ball at Greg Newsome after a touchdown on Tuesday, Harbaugh made sure the quarterback was penalized 15 yards for taunting. You can be sure the topic was addressed during the team’s Tuesday night film session. “We have our team meeting, and all those plays come up, the different things come up. So, that’s an opportunity for coaching points. So, we went over the sequence, and everybody knows,” head coach John Harbaugh said. “So, it was good. He was great about it. He’s great about accepting responsibility and he’s a very accountable guy.” Dart responded by having a good day. He threw two interceptions, one a slightly off-target ball that safety Raheem Layne grabbed after Darnell Mooney batted it into the air, and the other a ball he tried to squeeze in to Calvin Austin that defensive back Elijah Campbell came away with. Despite that, Wednesday was probably Dart’s sharpest day of camp. Dalen Cambre — How did this young man catch only 10 passes as a college player? In his second season, Cambre has had an exceptional start to camp as he bids for one of the backup wide receiver spots. Cambre has made several highlight-reel catches in camp, including one Wednesday on a deep ball down the right sideline from Jameis Winston. “I see him make a circus catch every single day,” said Harbaugh. “And not just that, he’s doing all the other things. He’s doing special teams. He knows what he’s doing. He’s running great routes. I think he’s making a move. I think he’s done a great job and he’s got our attention.” Tae Banks — The Giants’ 2023 first-round pick has followed a solid spring with a good start to training camp, aside from a bad drop on an interception earlier this week. Banks is firmly in the mix in the competition for snaps opposite Paulson Adebo. Banks played collegiately at Maryland. Harbaugh, coach of the Baltimore Ravens for 18 years, was familiar with Banks before taking the Giants job. “We’ve known Tae for a long time. He’s from the area there, played at Maryland. We knew him coming out,” Harbaugh said. “I was really thrilled that he was on the team coming here. And I was excited to see how he did, and he’s done really well.” Dominic Zvada — The undrafted rookie placekicker took his turn in the kicking rotation with Ben Sauls on Wednesday. Zvada was a perfect 10 of 10 on field goals and extra points. Theo Johnson — The third-year tight end is a frustrating player. He will drop balls that look like they should be easy catches. Then, he will have days like Wednesday when he made two difficult catches with safety Tyler Nubin draped all over him. Calvin Austin — Like Cambre, he just keeps making plays every day. Losers Andrew Thomas — The star left tackle was not really a “loser”. Thomas, however, got yanked off the field for a play after committing a false start during a red zone session. In his media sessions, Harbaugh has not been critical of players for a high number of penalties. Taking Thomas off the field, though, shows that the veteran coach is not taking the penalties lightly. Theo Johnson under center — The Giants are experimenting with a Kansas City Chiefs-style sneak/Tush Push play with tight end Theo Johnson under center. They ran it Wednesday from their own 1-yard line. I hate, hate, hate, hate this play. It has disaster written all over it, and I hope we never see it during the regular season. Injury notes Edge defender Brian Burns and safety Beau Brade both sat out practice. Rookie wide receiver Malachi Fields only did individual work. Harbaugh said the injuries to all three players were “minor”, and that each would have played if Wednesday had been a game day. Nickel cornerback Dru Phillips left practice after a collision in the end zone with a wide receiver. I believe it was Xavier Gipson, but it was on the far end of the field blocked by players. Harbaugh said Phillips’ injury appeared to be minor, but the Giants would monitor him throughout the evening. Malik Nabers did his usual individual drills and routes on air. Wide receiver JuJu Smith-Schuster was a full practice participant a day after sitting out with knee swelling. Cornerback Jarrick Bernard-Converse was back to practice after missing a couple of days. Running back Cam Skattebo was not listed as injured, but did have a lighter workload on Wednesday. Roster moves As we reported earlier, the Giants made four roster moves . Defensive tacke Roy Robertson-Harris was placed on season-ending IR, ending hopes that he could return late this season. Second-year wide receiver Beaux Collins was waived. To fill those spots, the Giants added defensive backs D.J. James and David Long . Marty Mornhinweg pays a visit Marty Mornhinweg, former head coach of the Detroit Lions and a four-time NFL offensive coordinator, was on the field at Giants practice on Wednesday. Mornhingweg made the rounds, introducing himself to media members. Mornhingweg’s son, Skyler, is a football analyst for the Giants. Quote of the day “There’s absolutely nothing to do here. Beautiful place, but nothing to do here.” — Odell Beckham on West Virginia Mixing and matching The Giants did a lot of work on Wednesday with the units mixed up. Rather than first unit vs. first unit, there were a number of instances of the first team working against the second or third team. “You go ones against ones, you get good on good, just like you would expect. That’s more the coordinators calling what they want to call,” Harbaugh said. “If we go ones versus twos, we’re still, at this stage of camp, we’re still running our offense and defense. But the coordinator, if it’s the first offense, then he’s going to ask for some things. He wants to see more cover two, more cover three. He wants to see a blitz. He doesn’t want to see a blitz. He can help script that, but the defense still plays. It’s our calls, that kind of thing. “And then you also, we were able to run some longer periods out. So, you saw the guys out there for 12 plays, nine plays, for six no huddle plays, things like that, which become more game-like. So, that’s the balance I think of it.” Remaining Greenbrier practice schedule The Giants’ stay in West Virginia is winding down. There are only two more open practices. So, if you are in the area you are running out of chances to see your favorite team practice. Thursday, August 6 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Friday, August 7 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Saturday, August 8 — 10 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.

full_text: ﻿New York Giants defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris celebrates with pass rusher Brian Burns after sacking Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Geno Smith | Getty Images The New York Giants made four roster moves prior to practice on Wednesday, 8/5. The Giants announced that they’ve placed defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris on the injured reserve, as well as waiving wide receiver Beaux Collins with an injury designation. Those two moves create a pair of needed roster openings after the team signed cornerbacks David Long and DJ James . Long was originally drafted by the Los Angeles Rams out of Michigan in the 3rd round of the 2019 NFL Draft. He has adequate size and speed, at 5-foot-11, 196 pounds, with a 4.45-second 40 at the 2019 Combine, though he does have elite quickness, agility, and explosiveness. Long’s 3-cone drill (6.45 seconds) and short shuttle (3.97 seconds) were by far the best among corners at the 2019 Combine. Long bounced around the NFL after his first four seasons with the Rams, spending time with the Las Vegas Raiders, Green Bay Packers, Carolina Panthers (twice), and Indianapolis Colts. This is, in fact, Long’s second stint with the Giants, after he spent the 2024 off-season with the Giants before being waived in that year’s final roster cuts. DJ James was originally drafted out of Auburn in the 6th round of the 2024 draft by the Seattle Seahawks. James started his collegiate career at Oregon before transferring to Auburn and was a highly regarded corner at both schools. He’s undersized at 5-foot-11, 175 pounds, but has very good agility and short-area quickness, and he showed a good feel for both man and zone coverage in college. James was waived in the Seahawks’ final roster cuts and signed with the New England Patriots’ practice squad in 2024, which is where he also spent 2025. The Giants had previously hoped that DT Roy Robertson-Harris could return late in the season after suffering a torn Achilles early in the off-season. However, that hope has been put to rest and the Giants officially ended his season by placing him on the injured reserve prior to the start of the season. Robertson-Harris was a starter for the Giants in 2025 and was in line to compete for a starting job this year. WR Beaux Collins was competing for a spot as a reserve wide receiver and special teams player. He signed with the Giants as an undrafted free agent out of Notre Dame following the 2025 NFL Draft, and was the only undrafted player to make the team last year. Collins struggled with route running last year, but also became a favorite among fans after he generated highlight reel plays in camp and preseason games.

title: NY Giants’ safety Tyler Nubin hopes ‘opportunistic’ scheme unlocks ball skills
summary: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — New York Giants safety Tyler Nubin was a ballhawk while playing collegiately for Minnesota, with 13 interceptions, 11 passes defensed, and three forced fumbles in 55 games. That kind of production is why the Giants, who had seen safeties Julian Love and Xavier McKinney leave in free agency the previous […]
full_text: Tyler Nubin | Getty Images WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — New York Giants safety Tyler Nubin was a ballhawk while playing collegiately for Minnesota, with 13 interceptions, 11 passes defensed, and three forced fumbles in 55 games. That kind of production is why the Giants, who had seen safeties Julian Love and Xavier McKinney leave in free agency the previous couple of offseasons, selected Nubin 47th in the 2024 NFL Draft. The production has not translated. In 26 games over two seasons, Nubin has just three passes defensed, one fumble recovery, and no interceptions. Nubin said Tuesday that he is hoping defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson’s scheme, similar to what he was asked to do at Minnesota, will lead to better production. #NYGiants safety Tyler Nubin discusses his offseason weight loss. — Ed Valentine (@edvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-08-05T16:25:11.654Z “It’s (Wilson’s scheme) great, man. It gives you a lot of opportunity to make plays. You got your eyes on the quarterback, and I think that’s something that I do very well, so something I’m really comfortable with, something I did a lot in college, so it’s going to be good,” Nubin said on Tuesday. “I think Dennard always has opportunistic defenses, looking back where he’s been, because they attack, and they make the offense think, gets them on their heels a little bit, whether that’s with the disguises or how we’re playing things, certain concepts. We can have our eyes on the quarterback and really go attack the football, so yeah, I think it’s definitely going to give me a really good opportunity for sure.” Wilson’s coverage scheme is zone-based, using a lot of two-high safeties, quarters coverage, and cornerbacks aggressively pressing wide receivers at the line of scrimmage. Nubin was asked to explain how zone-based coverage, often thought of as softer than man-to-man coverage, can be considered an attacking style. “Because it’s aggressive, man, especially when you have corners who can cover, especially when you have linebackers like we have. (Inside linebacker) Tremaine (Edmunds) and (inside linebacker) Arvell (Reese), who’s going to make that ball sail over the top.” Nubin said. “It allows you to be more aggressive on keying into the quarterback and where he’s going and jumping routes, whether that’s across the middle, whether that’s deep post routes, going to the post. So, it just allows you to go attack the football.” Nubin, whose athleticism has been pointed to by some as a possible reason for some of his struggles with play-making and tackling, lost eight pounds this offseason. He is back to his rookie playing weight of 205 pounds. “Just speed, man,” Nubin said when asked why he shed the weight. “I think my rookie year I played at like 205. Last year I was at like 213, 214. And right now, I’m like 205, 206, around there. So, I just wanted more for speed. I feel like I’m the strongest I’ve ever been, best shape I’ve ever been. So, I like this weight. I think I’m moving well.” Nubin has yet to make any big plays on the ball during camp. He and the Giants, though, are hopeful those will come. “I think he’s doing a good job. I do like the way he’s practicing. He’s a very determined, very serious-minded guy. He really wants to do well,” said head coach John Harbaugh. “He thinks about everything. He asks all the right questions. Sometimes you want to just say, “Hey, it’s not that complicated.” But you appreciate that about a player like that. So, I expect him to get back to where he was in college with the ball production. That would be great. “I’d love to see him get his hands on a lot of footballs.”

title: Isaiah Likely wants to show Giants made ‘right choice’ by signing him
summary: It wasn’t a surprise when John Harbaugh started bringing players he coached with the Baltimore Ravens to the New York Giants in free agency. After all, while Harbaugh believed that the Giants’ roster was close to competing, he still wanted players who were steeped in his culture to help him build a winning culture in […]
full_text: New York Giants tight end Isaiah Likely during practice. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It wasn’t a surprise when John Harbaugh started bringing players he coached with the Baltimore Ravens to the New York Giants in free agency. After all, while Harbaugh believed that the Giants’ roster was close to competing, he still wanted players who were steeped in his culture to help him build a winning culture in New York. The crown jewel of that free agent class is tight end Isaiah Likely , who the Baltimore Ravens drafted out of Coastal Carolina University in the fourth round of the 2022 NFL Draft. Likely spent the next four years as Baltimore’s second tight end, living in the shadow of All-Pro tight end Mark Andrews. But while he never quite got enough of an opportunity to establish himself as a star, he did earn Harbaugh’s admiration — enough so that the Giants made Likely one of the highest-paid tight ends in the NFL despite never eclipsing 45 receptions or 480 yards in a season. “I sure hope he’s a big weapon,” Harbaugh said. “I hope he’s a guy that makes a bunch of plays for us. That’s why we brought him here.” Likely gave props to Andrews for helping him develop. “He’s taught me a lot since I’ve come in the league,” Likely said following Tuesday’s practice. “Being able to just understand zones, to be able to just go out there, run freely and just let my talent shine. So, I feel like Mark’s brought me to the point now where I feel like being myself, being a star caliber tight end that I see myself being.” Likely was never a particularly productive tight end for the Ravens, but he did develop a good chemistry with quarterback Lamar Jackson and the two routinely hooked up when the play went off-script. That experience should help Likely establish a rapport with Giants’ quarterback Jaxson Dart, who likewise embraces chaos. “They’re both dogs,” Likely said. “And I’d say, with Jax [Dart], it’s really just having him understand the defense, really just letting his talent shine and showing that he’s really a capable franchise quarterback to be able to play against any defense if necessary.” In addition to his experience with an athletic quarterback who loves to freelance, Likely has plenty of experience with the type of offenses that Harbaugh likes to see his teams run. In particular, Likely’s rookie season was with Greg Roman calling the plays. Roman has rejoined John Harbaugh in New York after spending the last two seasons with Jim Harbaugh as the Los Angeles Chargers. Roman is now a senior offensive assistant for the Giants and seems to be in charge of designing the Giants’ run game. “I’d say there’s similarities in the run game,” Likely said of what Roman schemed in 2022. “Obviously, G-Ro’s a wizard, best of the best when it comes to the run.” That year the Ravens had one of the best running games in the NFL, ranking second in total yardage, yards per game, and yards per attempt, as well as fourth in rushing EPA while being seventh in rushing attempts. But, Likely continues, the offense won’t be just Roman’s work. Rather it will be a complex confection that draws on elements from across the Giants’ offensive coaching staff — a staff that features four former offensive coordinators. Matt Nagy is in charge of the offense, but part of his job is being the mixologist who balances the input of his assistants. As Likely says, the Giants offense is, “Just taking the flavors of just coaching from Coach Nagy [offensive coordinator Matt Nagy], Coach TK [tight ends coach Tim Kelly], [quarterbacks] Coach [Brian] Callahan, Coach Greg Roman as well. And then all just trying to make it our offense.” It’s a (potentially) heady mix of philosophies and perspectives that could yield a relatively unique offense in New York. The goal, Likely says, is to make every play look identical and give opposing defenses as few clues as to their intentions as possible. After all, if defenses aren’t sure what’s coming, they play slower and are less able to stop it. “Whether it’s running, pass, making everything look alike and putting the best players in situations to win,” Likely said. “Obviously trying to keep everything as simple as possible so you don’t have to think a lot when you’re out there. But dressing [the offense] up to the defense to make it look like exotic, creativity and be able to put the best players in the best situation to win.” Running back Tyrone Tracy says that Matt Nagy calls the concept “Elegant Simplicity.” Unfortunately, the offense hasn’t found much traction just yet in practice. That could be viewed as a concern regarding the offense, or a good sign for the Giants’ defense. The Giants’ defensive front has been consistently dominant in practice, and the secondary has been disruptive on the back end. “I feel like no matter who you put out there, they have a job to do,” Likely said. “And Coach Dennard [defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson] out there, he’s telling them every day to compete. Nobody has a guaranteed spot every day. I mean, every day is a new day. “And they know that when they’re out there, when they see nine [Likely’s number], when they see anybody out there, I’m going to give you the best look that you can get. So, I feel like that’s the competing aspect of training camp. And that’s going to help us during the season.” Ultimately, Likely understands that while he might be the crown jewel of the Giants’ free agent class, he’s just one part of the team, one of 11 players on the field. He believes that if he does his job to the best of his ability, he’ll prove the Giants’ faith in him. “I come out every day telling myself just win your one-eleventh every play, and whether it has run or pass matchups, whether it’s zone or man. And I feel like, if I win my one-eleventh, whether it’s I got to go against safety, linebacker, the end, corner, just giving Jax the best possibility to throw the ball or running back to be able to run in space.” The end result? “Going out there every day and [showing] everybody that when the Giants got me, they [made] the right choice.”

full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - DECEMBER 07: Jaylen Waddle #17 of the Miami Dolphins catches a pass for a touchdown during the NFL 2025 game against Brandon Stephens #21 of the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on December 07, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey."" (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning Gang Green Nation! Sometimes you just have to chuckle at the absurd level of hype training camp provides. If you scroll down to the last link in today’s Flight Connections you come to an article titled “Brandon Stephens is quickly giving Jets fans a reason to forget about Sauce Gardner.” Ummm … what?! Brandon Stephens is a 28 year old journeyman who probably shouldn’t be starting in the NFL. For his career Stephens has allowed a 105+ passer rating in coverage. No quarterback in the history of the NFL has a 105+ career passer rating. Which means throwing at Stephens essentially turns the average NFL quarterback into the best quarterback of all time. Last year Stephens allowed an ungodly 134+ passer rating, the worst of his NFL career, so it’s not like he’s on the upswing in his career. Sauce Gardner is a two time All Pro. He has allowed a passer rating of 76.7 for his career. Last season the 32nd ranked NFL passer was Joe Flacco, with a 79.2 passer rating. Throwing at Gardner essentially turns the average NFL starting quarterback into worse than the worst starting quarterback in the NFL. So here’s what we have. Throw at Stephens, get results better than the best QB in NFL history. Throw at Sauce, get results worse than the worst starting quarterback in the NFL. But sure, a few decent Stephens practices in August no doubt will make Jets fans forget about their former two time All Pro cornerback. Makes perfect sense when you really think about it. The irony here is that even the author of that article doesn’t believe his own headline. Read past the headline and you see he doesn’t even try to make the case his headline implies. He knows better than that. He just wanted to put up a clickbait headline full of absurd hype, because clicks are apparently more important than not misleading your audience. Sigh.
